title: Americans Are Spending More Money to Drive Worse Cars
excerpt: For the first time since the dawn of the automobile, the majority of new cars are not powered exclusively by gasoline: So far in 2026, electric vehicles and hyb
body: For the first time since the dawn of the automobile, the majority of new cars are not powered exclusively by gasoline: So far in 2026, electric vehicles and hybrids are outselling traditional gas-powered cars
As oil prices have gone up and up since the start of the war in Iran, drivers from Hanoi to Hamburg are picking up EVs like never before
According to the energy think tank Ember, 49 countries have broken EV-sales records this year
The prime minister of Thailand recently ditched his Rolls-Royce and commuted to work in an all-electric BYD Sealion
For all the angst over high gas prices, EVs accounted for just 6.4 percent of new-car sales in the U.S. from July to September
That’s a slight rise from January, before the beginning of the war with Iran—but just barely
The U.S. has long been something of an EV laggard, full of drivers ( and a president ) who are skeptical of battery-powered cars
But even as gas prices have jumped from $3 to $4.50 over the past year, drivers won’t budge
America’s car fleet was never going to flip overnight

No one forks over $50,000 for a Tesla the moment gas hits $5 a gallon. “If gas prices are higher for a little while,” Elaine Buckberg, a senior fellow at Harvard University’s Salata Institute for Climate and Sustainability and a former executive at General Motors, told me. “People say, ‘Oh, this is going to pass
I’m not going to go and change what vehicle I own.’” But when high gas prices linger for half a year or longer, Buckberg added, the direction of the car industry can shift
The shortages and lines of the 1970s helped kill the mid-century land yacht
In the 2000s, record-high gas prices tempered the craze for gas-guzzling SUVs and pushed millions of Americans to buy hybrids like the Toyota Prius
Now drivers have a real alternative to the whims of the world oil market
Americans are not all gasoline loyalists who’ve forsworn battery power
In fact, most drivers now say that they are strongly considering an EV as their next vehicle, and the trend is even stronger among people under 35
Pre-owned EVs are surging, but they represent a sliver of the used-car market, because so few of them are out there
The biggest winner from the gasoline spike has been the plain old hybrid, the green-car solution of the George W
Sales in the U.S. have jumped 27 percent over the past year
To some degree, Americans aren’t making the leap for several long-standing reasons: EVs are too expensive, and the options are lacking
Because the U.S. effectively bans electric cars made in China, we are cut off from buying something such as the BYD Dolphin Surf, an electric sedan that sells for about $22,000 in Europe
Many of the models that drivers are familiar with still cannot be had as an EV
Toyotas such as the RAV4 and Camry now come only as hybrids; last year, Ford killed the electric version of the F-150 pickup truck, this country’s most popular vehicle, citing low sales
Ford is now hyping up a roughly $30,000 electric pickup truck, but that won’t arrive until 2027
Meanwhile, America’s only electric minivan is the struggling Volkswagen ID
Buzz, a modern take on the flower-power bus
And although Tesla’s cars have a lot going for them, plenty of Americans say they won’t touch the brand because of Elon Musk
In short, the EV market is full of holes. [ Read: The great Tesla sell-off ] That said, it’s hard not to look at tepid EV sales and wonder whether Americans have lost the plot on electric cars
The price gap between gas and electric cars is closing; more EVs are now available for under $40,000
Charging networks are expanding, and battery ranges are climbing
Compared with even just a year or two ago, buying an electric car comes with fewer trade-offs
And in plenty of ways, EVs are just better
They don’t require much of the routine maintenance, such as oil changes, that make car ownership annoying

They can do all sorts of things that fossil-fuel burners cannot: refuel at home, keep a house’s lights on during a blackout, store luggage in a “frunk.” But if gas that’s creeping up on $5 a gallon isn’t enough to persuade people to go electric, what will? When I posed the question to Buckberg, she told me about research she’d worked on while at GM: Drivers were “happy to buy an EV—as long as they don’t have to give up anything they like about their current vehicle,” she said
In other words, it’s not enough for EVs to be good at what they’re good at—especially when relatively few Americans know someone who has one
They need to match the things that gas cars are good at too
Fast chargers are spreading, but not fast enough to free us from the mental load of worrying about where to refuel—something that’s been a given in a nation with a gas station at every corner
And what EVs can’t do yet ( unless you’re in China ) is recharge in as little time as it takes to pump gas

That’s something American drivers see as a prerequisite, even though most of us don’t regularly take very long road trips and drive an average of 30-some miles a day—a total easily handled by charging at home
There’s every reason to think that EVs will continue a gradual climb, Corey Cantor, the research director at the Zero Emission Transportation Association, told me

title: What Trump’s Comments About France Say About Him
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
You might imagine that, given the imminent midterm elections, a spluttering war in Iran, and his sinking personal approval , Donald Trump has enough to worry about
The president has been posting prolifically on Truth Social over the past two days about protests in France. “The migrants have taken over France
They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!” he wrote this morning
Trump’s reactions don’t tell us a great deal about the protests or about French society, but they do reveal three things about Trump
Even as the world’s most powerful man, he frequently seems to prefer watching TV and shooting opinions from the hip to engaging in governance

This explains why he continued to give freewheeling briefings, full of his own speculation and medical advice, while the coronavirus swept the United States in 2020, and it might be one reason he’s fixated on France at a time of political peril for his own party
Second, and related, Trump can’t resist meddling in other countries’ affairs, engaging in behavior that previous presidents would have concluded was inappropriate
The U.S. government has long worked to covertly influence foreign elections, and in some cases encouraged or fomented coups
But presidents have mostly avoided issuing public endorsements or other interventions in partisan politics overseas, two things Trump loves to do

He endorsed the prime minister of Japan for reelection, backed a right-wing candidate for president of Poland, placed tariffs on Brazil for prosecuting his ally Jair Bolsonaro, and lent his administration’s credibility to the reelection campaign of Hungary’s then-President Viktor Orbán. (Orbán lost.) This weekend, he endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu

Trump’s blaming of immigrants in France amplifies the platform of National Rally, a far-right party with fascist roots that is ideologically aligned with MAGA and has its best shot yet at capturing the French presidency for the first time next spring
But U.S. interference abroad tends to produce some pushback
Leaders and voters in sovereign countries may not like a superpower telling them how to live—especially in a nation such as France, which still sees itself as a global player

Apologists might contend that Trump’s meddling in foreign politics is a sign of strength, projecting American power worldwide, but the brush-off Trump received when begging for international assistance in the Persian Gulf showed the cost of treating allies dismissively

Trump’s approach to the protests is notable because for years, he seemed to get along with French President Emmanuel Macron better than with almost any other foreign leader, a bromance sealed with history’s most awkward handshake

Their friendship seems to have cooled more recently, in part because of tariffs and Trump’s antagonism toward Ukraine . (Notably, the Kremlin is also using France’s protests to score political points.) Third, Trump views all forms of protest—at least those with which he disagrees—as inherently illegitimate

The violence in France warrants concern: This past weekend, the country saw some of its worst riots in decades; shops were looted and landmarks were destroyed as rioters seemed to take advantage of the mass marches
But in his posts on Truth Social, the president does not simply condemn the violence—he suggests that the riots must be the work of foreign seditionists
The protest movement was in fact sparked by domestic concerns, particularly demands for better funding for the nation’s school system

Macron, in contrast to Trump, has said that many protestors have legitimate demands, even as he has fiercely condemned violence, which he blames on “troublemakers from far-left fringe groups.” Authoritarians see any popular resistance as a danger to their power, which is why the autocratic Russian regime and the aspiring strongman Trump are united in condemning French demonstrations

And as nationalists, they must also blame the danger on outsiders, even though French authorities have not made any link between immigrants and unrest. “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion,” Vice President Vance posted on X this weekend, along with a clip of the city hall in Limoges, in the old province of Limousin, burning. “They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility
They were told it would lead to this and they didn’t listen.” This was not only a missed opportunity for Vance to blame literal limousine liberals for the riots; it was patently absurd
The French don’t need outsiders to teach them how to rage in the streets

They’ve been doing it for centuries. (Trump, an aficionado of Les Misérables , might not have made this mistake .) To the extent that migrants are involved in these protests, it is proof that they have assimilated fully to the French way of life
Suggesting that Trump and Vance might be wiser to focus on getting their own house in order than to look overseas would be easy, but it misses the point

This weekend, while Trump was posting about French protests, Americans were participating in thousands of “No Kings” demonstrations around the country and Trump’s “border czar” was insinuating that Ilhan Omar, a Democratic lawmaker who is a naturalized citizen, committed immigration fraud
Trump’s attempts to delegitimize protest and whip up xenophobia aren’t ultimately about France

title: Two Firefighters Died in Yosemite—For What?
excerpt: This year, the Trump administration gave federal firefighters a mandate: no more letting fires burn
body: This year, the Trump administration gave federal firefighters a mandate: no more letting fires burn
Conventional wisdom among firefighters and public-land managers has held that allowing fires in remote areas to run their course can be beneficial

Wildland Fire Service was to pursue a policy of “full suppression” on every wildfire, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum instructed his workforce, to avoid the possibility of dangerous spread. “Accelerate initial attack,” Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins put it in her own directive to the Forest Service. “Suppress fires early and limit growth.” And when Yosemite National Park caught on fire last month, that is what firefighters did
The hazy skies above the park filled with aircraft—planes dropping fire retardant on forested slopes; helicopters ferrying hotshot crews to the blaze

At one point, at least 17 helicopters were in rotation, along with more than 1,000 firefighters. “I’ve worked in Yosemite and with Yosemite for almost 40 years,” Tom Nichols, a former head of fire and aviation for the National Park Service (and no relation to the Atlantic writer Tom Nichols), told me. “I’ve never seen that kind of response.” At the start, attacking the fire aggressively made sense: It had started near a popular hiking trail and was burning on a slope above Wawona, a small community in the park
In such situations, federal policy, even before this year, called for firefighters to use “full suppression” to try to put it out as quickly as possible, former Yosemite fire officials told me
But as it developed, the Dome Fire spread to the north and east, farther up the mountains, away from any homes or communities
The resources being poured into fighting it began to baffle some fire veterans

As a former Yosemite official put it to me, “There’s really no reason to be attacking a fire like that.” (I spoke with several sources for this story who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly and hoped to avoid professional repercussions.) Such an aggressive approach can be dangerous
Five days into the effort to put it out, one of the helicopters was doing water-bucket drops from a nearby lake when it crashed
Both pilots died . “For what?” one federal fire official told me. “There’s nothing out there

Just let nature do its thing.” Another official had to ask: “Did they die in vain?” Under the Trump administration’s policy of full fire suppression, so far this year entrapments—when firefighters’ positions are surrounded by flames—are above the average for the previous two decades
At least 17 wildland firefighters, pilots, and contractors have been killed, surpassing the full-year average over the past decade, according to the Wildland Firefighter Foundation
That number includes four firefighters in Colorado who died this summer responding to the Knowles and Gore fires as flames spread amid high winds and low visibility
After that incident, several Democratic senators called on the Interior Department to investigate whether the full-suppression policy put firefighters at undue risk
Brian Fennessy, the Wildland Fire Service chief, doesn’t think that the new policy is putting firefighters in more danger, he told me
The two pilots’ deaths in the Dome Fire were a tragedy—one he hopes his agency can learn from—but “this was not the year to allow managed fire on the landscape,” he said
The winter was historically warm, and snowpacks were at record lows across much of the western United States
Federal authorities were not about to let fires burn unattended, even in the wild

And the administration’s policy of suppression does mean increasing the number of people and helicopters fighting a given fire, he said: “Instead of two engines and a helicopter, maybe you’ve got four engines, two helicopters, maybe an air tanker.” Given how hot and dry it’s been, had firefighters not focused on putting out fires, in Yosemite and elsewhere, many could have been worse, he said
The question of whether to harness or extinguish fire is particularly relevant in Yosemite

This is where America’s formal debate over that policy began, after Abraham Lincoln signed a bill in 1864 to grant the Yosemite Valley and the Mariposa Grove of giant sequoias to California as a public trust
The commission to oversee the area disagreed about the question of annual burning by Native Americans, Stephen Pyne, a historian of fire, told me

Fires set by the Ahwahneechees were “deliberate and purposeful, even artful,” Pyne writes in his book about Yosemite’s fire history, Pyrocene Park : “They burned to keep grasslands open and attract game animals like deer to fresh forage; to keep trees from crowding out annual-grass prairies; to help harvest acorns; to stimulate willows useful for basketry; to promote berries.” Some of the Yosemite’s first commissioners saw the value in that

Others, such as Frederick Law Olmsted, considered such fires vandalism that undermined, as he put it, “the duty of preservation.” For more than a century afterwards, the suppressionists prevailed until, in 1974, Yosemite leaders allowed a major lightning-caused fire to burn in the Illilouette Creek basin, whose creek runs behind Half Dome, the park’s famous bald mountain
This was the first big test of its new policy to manage certain fires for ecological benefit
Since then, more than 100 fires have come through that basin, and scientists have documented its renaissance
The proportion of the basin covered by dense conifer forest fell by 20 percent, and a mosaic of meadows and grasslands emerged
Biodiversity bloomed, as bees and bats and understory plants thrived
Even streams flowed a bit more abundantly, as fewer trees competed for water and snow had more open space to accumulate, Scott Stephens, a professor of wildfire science at UC Berkeley, told me
The regular burning also makes the basin more capable of handling future fire, he said, by minimizing how much of it burns at a destructive intensity
It’s now “one of the most resilient, functioning forests in all of California.” Set under the right conditions, prescribed fires, too, can help prevent hotter-burning conflagrations
The evidence was plain just four years ago in Yosemite, when the Washburn Fire bore down on the Mariposa Grove and its revered giant sequoias
The park had conducted more than 20 prescribed fires in that area since the 1970s

And when the Washburn Fire approached the grove, the flames moved around the treated areas as if they were boulders in a stream, sparing the sequoias that have been burning up in great numbers elsewhere in California
But this year, at least, under the Trump administration’s leadership, the park seems to have stepped back from prescribed burns as well

Although in many recent years Yosemite has done several prescribed fires, this year the park has done none and even canceled a long-planned prescribed fire near the Mariposa Grove scheduled for May, around Memorial Day, according to two people familiar with the decision

They added that Ray McPadden, the superintendent of the park, was concerned it would affect park visitation because it required closing parts of the grove temporarily. (McPadden did not respond to a request for comment; the Wildland Fire Service said Yosemite was looking for an opportunity to complete the burn this fall.) Over the long term, avoiding fire puts the sequoias at risk, Cicely Muldoon, who retired as Yosemite’s superintendent last year, told me

And on top of that, jettisoning controlled burns, which ultimately keep fires modest, also means that “you’re really putting people in harm’s way.” A little fire—however it starts—can help prevent future huge fires
Under the Trump administration’s reorganization of federal firefighting resources, superintendents of national parks no longer decide how to manage fires that start within their borders

title: Why the Internet Needs a Memory
excerpt: In 1996, during the early years of the web, I could see that those of us who were participating online were creating an extraordinary new record of human activi
body: In 1996, during the early years of the web, I could see that those of us who were participating online were creating an extraordinary new record of human activity—and allowing it to disappear almost as quickly as we made it
The web was becoming the place where government officials made promises, journalists published information in the public interest, and ordinary people shared ideas and documented their lives
Yet it was fragile—equal parts consequential and ephemeral
Many people assume that once something is published online, it will remain forever retrievable
The saying that “the internet never forgets” has produced a dangerously false sense of permanence
In reality, the internet forgets continuously
Websites are constantly revised, deleted, and abandoned altogether
This is why, 30 years ago, I founded the Internet Archive
I wanted to build a mechanism for permanence in the internet age

Soon after that, I helped build the Internet Archive’s most-used resource, the Wayback Machine, a system that would preserve webpages as they appeared at any one moment in time, allowing future readers to return to those moments
The idea was simple but urgent: If the internet was going to become humanity’s principal publishing platform, then it needed what every great publishing system that came before it had needed
People all over the world use the Wayback Machine all the time
What began as an effort to preserve the web has become an essential tool for journalists, researchers, historians, and the broader public
Yet the future of this tool has become extremely vulnerable
The New York Times is now blocking the Internet Archive’s ability to preserve its articles
The Guardian has restricted our access to its published articles and removed articles from some of the Wayback Machine’s interfaces
USA Today and a growing number of other news organizations have also placed barriers in the path of web archivists (even, yes, The Atlantic )
As of May 2026, Harvard’s Nieman Journalism Lab had identified more than 340 local-news sites that were limiting the Internet Archive’s ability to preserve their journalism
The publishers taking these steps have all pointed to one reason: the unauthorized use of their work by AI companies to train large language models
They complain that our library serves as a back door around paywalls, licensing negotiations, and technical restrictions
The Times has said that it is blocking us because the Wayback Machine allegedly provides “unfettered access” to its work
But this fear-based approach does not take into account that the Internet Archive is taking steps to prevent AI companies from scraping the materials we preserve
Reporting requires skilled people, time, courage, legal support, and institutions willing to withstand pressure
Journalists have watched advertising revenue disappear and subscription growth slow while technology companies build enormously profitable products using material created by others
Publishers have every right to challenge commercial businesses that they believe are inappropriately exploiting their work
But blocking a nonprofit library is the wrong response to this problem
Impeding the Wayback Machine’s preservation work will not prevent powerful AI companies from gathering training data
It will certainly not restore the advertising-based business model that supported newspapers in the 20th century, a business model that has long since collapsed
What it will do is prevent historians, researchers, courts, ordinary readers—and, most ironic, journalists themselves—from consulting an accurate record of what once appeared on the web
It is difficult to quantify the scale of what we stand to lose

A continuous record of web activity is an enormously powerful accountability tool, especially at a time when seeking the truth and reporting it has become ever more complicated and the informational environment is growing only more complex

Joe Mullin, who is a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, has offered a fitting analogy: Imagine a newspaper announcing that physical libraries will no longer be permitted to preserve copies of its past issues
That is effectively what is happening now
For the past three decades, the Wayback Machine has served as a library for the public web
The destruction of that library is creating holes in the historical record
A crucial fact in this debate is one that publishers themselves know better than anyone: Journalists rely on the Wayback Machine

They use it to recover deleted tweets, verify past public statements by powerful individuals who wish to avoid scrutiny, examine earlier versions of government documents, and establish what a person or institution said about a subject before some controversy or scandal prompted them to change course
Journalists use the Wayback Machine to see defunct websites and the archives of closed newsrooms
They use it when the primary evidence for a story has vanished from the web
A news organization that blocks the Wayback Machine may believe it is acting in the best interest of its journalists

title: How Corruption Got This Bad
excerpt: “Isn’t that illegal?” That’s a question I get asked a lot as a former federal prosecutor
body: “Isn’t that illegal?” That’s a question I get asked a lot as a former federal prosecutor
Donald Trump, his family, and members of his administration are most often the inspiration
Defense Department a $400 million luxury jumbo jet for the president’s use, which he plans to take with him to his presidential library when he leaves office
Then Trump gave Qatar NATO-like security guarantees
Does that sound like a bribe? Exactly four days before Trump was inaugurated for the second time, the Emiratis invested $500 million in the Trump-family crypto business
Four months later, Trump green-lighted selling them advanced AI chips, which the Biden administration had blocked out of fear that they would fall into the hands of the Chinese
But even though I hear “Isn’t that illegal?” a lot more than I used to, it isn’t a new question

Former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy and former Virginia Governor Robert McDonnell, a Democrat and a Republican, both took lavish gifts from individuals and entities seeking their help and made national news when they were prosecuted for it
Surely that was illegal? Common sense notwithstanding, however, the answer is no
Neither Espy nor McDonnell was held accountable, and even Trump’s seemingly egregious misbehavior likely can’t be prosecuted
That’s because starting in the 1980s, the Supreme Court has interpreted anti-corruption laws in ways so narrow as to effectively legalize flat-out corruption
These decisions put whole categories of politicians’ conduct beyond a prosecutor’s reach
For 20 years, I prosecuted white-collar crime at the U.S

In between, I prosecuted on corruption charges the vice chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff; the mayor of Baltimore; the Baltimore police commissioner; the Baltimore City state’s attorney; and dozens of other politicians, government employees, police officers, and prison guards
I served in leadership positions at the Justice Department and on Capitol Hill focused on corruption

I finished my DOJ career in the department’s Public Integrity Section in Washington, the specialized unit that prosecuted public corruption around the country—until February 2025, when it was effectively shut down
I was one of the prosecutors asked to dismiss the case against New York Mayor Eric Adams
Like nearly all my colleagues in Public Integrity, I declined to do so and left the department that year
In all that time, I experienced how the Supreme Court restrained prosecutors in cases involving public officials
Even before the start of my career, the justices had begun to chip away at federal anti-corruption statutes, and this project accelerated during my tenure
When FBI agents brought me evidence of misconduct, I often had to turn the cases away, knowing I’d never be able to make charges stick
The longer I served, the harder my job became. [ Adam Serwer: Trump’s politicized prosecutions may hit a roadblock ] The first of these Supreme Court rulings was McNally v

In that case, a member of the Kentucky governor’s Cabinet, a local businessman, and a former chair of the Kentucky Democratic Party received hundreds of thousands of dollars in kickbacks from an insurance company that did business with the state
Prosecutors charged them with depriving the public of its right to their “honest services,” a crime under the federal mail- and wire-fraud statutes
The Court reversed their convictions and declared that the public enjoyed no such right

Although federal courts had upheld similar convictions for more than 40 years, the Supreme Court ruled that all those courts had gotten it wrong: It declared that the mail-fraud—and, by implication, the wire-fraud—statute was limited to protecting money and property, not intangible rights such as citizens’ right to good government
One year later, a broad bipartisan majority in Congress passed legislation effectively reversing the Court’s decision
Sun-Diamond Growers of California , the Supreme Court reversed the conviction of an agricultural trade association that gave gifts—tickets to the U.S
Open, expensive luggage, even a crystal bowl—to the U.S. secretary of agriculture in the Clinton administration
The Supreme Court held that giving a politician lavish gifts because of his official position was not illegal

Rather than focusing on the conduct at hand, Justice Antonin Scalia, writing for a unanimous Court, spun out a ridiculous hypothetical—that the government’s interpretation of the statute would allow the president to be prosecuted for accepting “replica jerseys given by championship sports teams.” What that claim ignored was the reality that no Justice Department would ever authorize such a prosecution
United States , decided in 2010, the Supreme Court reversed the conviction of Jeffrey Skilling, a former CEO of Enron Corporation, for conspiring to commit honest-services fraud
I had been one of the prosecutors in Skilling’s trial
Although Skilling was the president of a publicly traded company, not a politician, he was charged with conspiracy to commit honest-services wire fraud for undisclosed self-dealing
Self-dealing is a problem whether the perpetrator is a corporate executive hiding a conflict of interest from shareholders or an elected official hiding one from voters
Except the Supreme Court held that it wasn’t illegal

Confronted with the fact that lower courts had for years upheld honest-services-fraud convictions for undisclosed self-dealing, Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg’s majority opinion noted the “infrequency” of those decisions and how they were not “models of clarity.” That, of course, didn’t mean those decisions were wrong
Remarkably, Ginsburg didn’t even say they were
Instead, she claimed that because bribery and kickbacks were the “basis of most honest-services prosecutions,” that’s what the statute’s application would be limited to
In place of legal analysis, the Court resorted to a game of numbers, and the practical effect was to restrict the number of corruption cases prosecutors could bring under this statute

title: The Minimal Requirements for a Society Free From Fear
excerpt: In 1989, the year the West won the Cold War, Francis Fukuyama published an essay announcing “the end of history.” He wasn’t claiming that historic events would
body: In 1989, the year the West won the Cold War, Francis Fukuyama published an essay announcing “the end of history.” He wasn’t claiming that historic events would stop taking place; what was over, rather, was the debate about the meaning of those events
Since the Enlightenment, Western thinkers had believed that history was progressing toward a final destination
According to communism, the engine of progress was class conflict, and history would end in the creation of a classless society
With the failure of the Soviet empire, Fukuyama argued, this idea had been discredited

Only one alternative remained: It was now clear that the “end point of mankind’s ideological evolution” was “the universalization of Western liberal democracy as the final form of human government.” There would still be disagreements within liberalism—Fukuyama named religion and nationalism as likely fault lines—but there could no longer be any disagreement about liberalism

To see how that judgment is holding up, just look at the kinds of titles that political theorists are producing these days: How Liberalism Failed , A World After Liberalism , Liberalism Against Itself
Even Fukuyama wrote a book titled Liberalism and Its Discontents
Across the West, the far right and the far left are on the rise, and the one thing they agree on is their contempt for liberalism

To MAGA and its European cousins, such as France’s National Rally and the United Kingdom’s Reform Party, liberals are rootless elitists who look down on their fellow citizens while coddling immigrants and criminals
To progressives and democratic socialists, liberalism—often qualified with the prefix neo —means ruthless globalized capitalism, prettied up with rhetoric about meritocracy and human rights
Appeals to liberal principles and defenses of the liberal world order have shown little power to rally the public, or even much of the political establishment

Now that the liberal triumphalism of the post–Cold War era is dying, what can replace it? The answer may lie in another important essay written in 1989—one that received much less attention than Fukuyama’s, but enjoys a cult reputation among keepers of the liberal flame. “The Liberalism of Fear,” by Judith Shklar, has just been published for the first time as a book—a small book, because the essay is only about 8,000 words long, but a timely one

In fact, as the political scientist Mark Lilla says in his introduction, it’s “far more timely today than it was upon its publication.” In 1989, Shklar’s minimalist definition of liberalism as a bulwark against government terror—what she calls, simply, a politics of “damage control”—might have sounded unambitious or uninspiring
In an America where ICE agents shoot protesters and grab people off the street, it sounds prescient
Shklar’s argument involves history and philosophy, but like all political ideas, it begins with an intuition, a feeling
Communism, one might say, begins in indignation: a refusal to accept a world where some people exploit and others are exploited
Nationalism begins in loyalty: a sense of connection and obligation to one’s own people
There is nothing wrong with these emotions; they are even praiseworthy

But when one political feeling crowds out all others—when everyone and everything is subordinated to the pursuit of social justice or national pride—good can justify the worst evils. [ From the May 2022 issue: There is no liberal world order ] What makes liberalism different from these political ideologies is that, as Shklar writes, it “does not have any particular positive doctrines about how people are to conduct their lives.” Liberalism doesn’t offer a vision of a perfect world—one where injustice is abolished, or where a particular nation reigns supreme

Instead, it is rooted in a justified fear of the real world, where people with power often use it to oppress, torture, and kill. “Liberalism’s deepest grounding,” Shklar writes, is the belief “that cruelty is an absolute evil.” The classic liberal principles outlined by thinkers such as Locke and Mill, the ideas that guided the American and French Revolutions, follow from this basic fear of cruelty
Freedom of religion means that you won’t be burned at the stake for holding the wrong beliefs
Freedom of speech means that you won’t be locked up for saying what you think
The rule of law means that you can be punished only for committing a crime, not because a powerful person is out to get you

Not coincidentally, these liberal freedoms are framed as limits on the power of the state. “Public cruelty,” Shklar writes, “is made possible by differences in public power,” and the government is always more powerful than any citizen
This isn’t necessarily a bad thing; we want the government to have the power to punish crime or defend against invasion

But liberalism believes that there must be strict and effective limits on how that power is used. “The governments of this world, with their overwhelming power to kill, maim, indoctrinate, and make war are not to be trusted unconditionally,” Shklar writes

What the liberalism of fear wants to prevent above all are “habitual and pervasive acts of cruelty and torture performed by military, paramilitary, and police agents in any regime.” This might have seemed like an odd concern for an American political philosopher in 1989

Police states were disappearing in Eastern Europe; democracy activists were bravely standing up to tanks in Tiananmen Square; Nelson Mandela left his jail cell on his way to becoming president of South Africa
Bush had its problems, but no one would have put paramilitary violence and police torture high on the list

At a time when Fukuyama was celebrating the end of history, why was Shklar contemplating these specters at the feast? The most obvious answer is that, unlike most Americans, she had seen them firsthand
Born to a Jewish family in Latvia in 1928, Judith Nisse grew up in the shadow of approaching war and the Holocaust

In an autobiographical lecture, she recalled that as a child, she was traumatized by reading Shakespeare’s play Titus Andronicus , which is full of murder, cannibalism, and severed heads: “To this day I can still feel the fear and horror it inspired.” Her sister tried to comfort her by saying that “these things did not really happen,” but it didn’t help, because “both she and I knew that far worse was going on all around us.” As Jews in Latvia, Shklar recalled, “everyone around us wanted us to be somewhere else at best, or to kill us at worst.” The Nisse family managed to escape at the last possible moment and took an epic journey in 1940 across Russia and the Pacific to Canada
The next year, the Nazis invaded Latvia and the 40,000 Jews of Riga were murdered, most of them shot by German troops and local auxiliaries in a nearby forest

When Shklar arrived at Harvard’s department of government as a graduate student in 1951, she was struck by how completely her American colleagues ignored the central political experience of their own time: “I knew what had happened in Europe between 1940 and 1945, and I assumed that most people at Harvard also were aware of the physical, political, and moral calamity that had occurred, but it was never to be discussed.” This “isolating” experience “had a lot to do with my later writings,” Shklar noted

At first, she didn’t intend to stay in the academy: “I would have liked to be a literary editor of The Atlantic or some such publication.” But she remained at Harvard for her entire career as a professor, writing about subjects directly or indirectly connected with the European catastrophe: the failure of the Enlightenment tradition, the concept of law in the Nuremberg trials, the nature of cruelty and injustice. “The Liberalism of Fear” was published three years before Shklar’s death in 1992, and though it wasn’t one of her major works, the title has become a kind of shorthand for her worldview

As Lilla writes in his introduction, for Shklar, “fear of being in another’s arbitrary power is the ur-human experience that modern liberalism was developed to stave off.” In the essay, she discusses the tools that modern liberal societies use for this purpose

Some of these tools are legal: “Without well-defined procedures, honest judges, opportunities for counsel and for appeals, no one has a chance.” Others are political and economic, such as security for private property: “Nothing gives a person greater social resources than legally guaranteed proprietorship.” [ Read: This is the way a world order ends ] But Shklar is most concerned with the ideas and habits of mind that sustain liberal societies
And it is here that her message for today becomes most urgent
The “perfect liberal,” she writes, “respects other people without condescension, arrogance, humility, or fear

He or she does not insult others with lies or cruelty, both of which mar one’s own character no less than they injure one’s victims.” These aren’t the heroic virtues needed to win wars or found empires; they are minimal requirements for a society free from fear

title: Making the internet better for AI agents might make it worse for everyone else
excerpt: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
body: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
To get stories like this in your inbox first,  sign up here
Until recently, you could divide internet users into just two categories: bots and people
Websites have long allowed bots to perform automated tasks, like capturing the content of web pages, but rules govern what they can access and how they behave
The web, after all, is designed primarily for people, even if we occasionally have to solve puzzles and captchas to prove we are not bots
But this is being entirely upended by the release of personal AI agents, which can do things for you online, like booking flights or hotel rooms
They have recently been unleashed at scale by the launch of apps like OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse

Muse was downloaded 5 million times in its first month, and agentic web traffic tripled from August to September.  The mingling of these agents with human visitors—on an internet designed largely to prioritize people—has gone poorly, with many websites blocking AI agents that consumers have sent to negotiate prices or plan vacations

Still, if the demand for agents keeps going up, the internet will be increasingly redesigned for them instead of us.  Such changes are coming because agents really do mark a third category of web visitor
They’re not humans, of course, and they use the internet at machine speed
But they’re not quite bots, either, because they’re acting on behalf of individual people to do tasks that can be perfectly legitimate and useful

They just work faster than a person would.  Since agents don’t fit into the systems we have for differentiating bots from people, some platforms (especially the more security-conscious ones) have opted to just ban them entirely
TechCrunch recently reported people having trouble deploying their agents to websites ranging from Pizza Hut to Yelp, which doesn’t allow AI to book restaurant reservations
Amazon has blocked Muse’s agents and is waging a court battle against the AI startup Perplexity to block its agents too

Though a judge recently ruled in favor of Perplexity, Amazon has filed an appeal in which it argues that AI agents threaten its advertising business by making it harder to distinguish between ads seen by humans and those served to bots
These blocks are annoying for early adopters, but Ethan Mollick, an associate professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, predicts it will soon affect the whole web

Once it becomes common knowledge that AI agents can be sent to request refunds or negotiate prices, for example, agents will overwhelm customer service departments to the point where they become unusable by real people. “Humans will eventually get very annoyed when their agents aren’t allowed to do this on their behalf,” he recently wrote on LinkedIn
If demand for personal agents grows, platforms will find ways to let them in

That’s especially true because the vast majority of agentic web traffic is to e-commerce sites, meaning that platforms have money to be made if they allow the legions of new AI agents to shop on behalf of real people
Indeed, the e-commerce giant Shopify is already welcoming the agents by giving them their own checkout lanes that bypass pages designed for humans
The pressing question is what will happen to the internet for the rest of us in the process
We’ve grown used to a web where, even as it’s increasingly designed to exploit our attention, humans have at least remained the intended users
But that internet might yield to one optimized instead for the agents that will eventually outnumber us, making it even more miserable for the humans who are left
How might this go? Perhaps websites become increasingly neglected as destinations for real people
Humans who want to browse and compare products themselves encounter worse interfaces
Verification systems are imperfect; imagine constantly being asked to verify that you’re a human, not an agent (and hey, maybe you’ll need to get your iris scanned to do so)
That sweater you want doesn’t have one price listed for everyone but instead displays different prices to different people’s agents
You can never tell when your agent’s recommendation is influenced by advertisements or platform commissions
That’s a far cry from the future promised by Google , Anthropic , and OpenAI , in which AI agents will give consumers greater power and bargaining leverage

Agents are capable of genuinely helping people by fighting bogus medical bills or researching more affordable car insurance, for example.  Whether they can actually be used for these purposes depends on what rules are set for how agents interact with websites and what exactly they’re allowed to do.  These rules are still being written

Some of them will benefit all of us—neither consumers nor businesses want credit card information to be waved around by agents wherever they roam the web, for example, and rules to keep agents more secure are a good thing

It’s the more contested ones, like whether businesses can block agents from their websites or prevent them from negotiating better deals for consumers, that will determine whether the web becomes a highway for agents working for us or against us.

title: “We were looking at it wrong”: The explosive claim that’s upended the AI world
excerpt: A hopeful bombshell: Researcher Nick Cammarata published a 26,000-word claim that AI models may be far easier to understand than previously thought—sparking bot
body: A hopeful bombshell: Researcher Nick Cammarata published a 26,000-word claim that AI models may be far easier to understand than previously thought—sparking both celebration and serious skepticism across the field
We were looking at it wrong: What seemed like tangled, unreadable neural networks may actually follow a hidden logic
A neuron that fired for both cats and cars wasn't confused—it was detecting V-shapes

Not everyone is convinced: Prominent researchers warn that neurons are just one tiny piece of a much larger puzzle, and that researchers currently understand less than 0.01% of how top AI models actually work

Hope over hype: Cammarata himself admits people took his findings too far—but argues the AI safety community, starved for optimism, needed a reminder that understanding these systems isn't necessarily impossible. " data-chronoton-post-id="1147149" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> “I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration
Cammarata’s claim is that LLMs might in fact be far easier to understand—and thus to monitor and control—than people previously thought
If true (and we’ll come back to that), it’s a huge deal

After a summer filled with revelations that swarms of agents built by top firms like OpenAI and Anthropic have been breaking their containment and causing havoc on the public internet—often while those companies weren’t aware of what their agents were up to—the AI industry is desperate to get a better handle on the technology it has built

That’s one reason the blog post landed with such force. “I think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history,” one AI researcher posted on X : “I feel like my understanding of what a neural net is has been catapulted into the future by five years or something.” Another called it “the most important AI paper of the year.” Not everyone is convinced, however

What Cammarata has shared is little more than a hunch, says Chris Potts at Stanford University, who leads a team that is trying to understand how LLMs work. “As far as I can tell, nothing about this blog post makes the problems any easier,” he says. “It would not have occurred to me to say this at all, but very prominent people on social media seem to believe that it is an all-encompassing breakthrough.” I talked to Cammarata the day after his post blew up

He says he was surprised by the response: “I didn’t expect people to update [their beliefs about AI] quite as much as they did.”  “I just really enjoy looking at neural networks,” he says. “Honestly, I really like doing this stuff

And after looking a lot, I have a hopeful story.” Knotted networks It has long been accepted that the mechanisms inside neural networks, the software that underpins most AI models, are very hard—perhaps impossible—to unpick fully
That’s because when the networks are trained, they appear to take on weird, tangled structures that make no sense to a human
Researchers like to say today’s AI is grown like a garden, not built like a bridge
Cammarata has done more than most to establish that view
He previously worked at OpenAI, where he helped pioneer techniques that allowed researchers to peer inside models, including tools that can probe individual neurons to see what they represent

It’s a little like how neuroscientists use MRI to study brains. ( MIT Technology Review chose this approach, known as mechanistic interpretability, as one of its 10 hottest technologies of 2025 .)   Back in 2020, Cammarata and his colleagues were studying a small image-recognition model called Inception v1
When they looked at its neurons, it seemed to be using them to capture multiple things at once
For example, they found that one neuron responded to both images of cars and images of cats
The researchers concluded that the model was getting at least some of its neurons to multitask, perhaps so that it could fit in more data
Looking at other models appeared to back this up
The phenomenon became known as superposition: Models folded unrelated concepts into single neurons
The upshot was clear: When you looked inside a model, what you saw was a vast, tangled knot
Most mechanistic interpretability research has therefore focused on ways to untangle that knot
But despite a few breakthroughs , progress has been slow
Today’s models, such as the latest LLMs, are so large and complex that researchers can make sense of only tiny pieces at a time
Some leading figures in the field doubt if it will ever be possible to understand an LLM in fine-grained detail
Cammarata was one of them. “I was very pessimistic,” he says
But then he took the trouble to really look
Nothing but neurons At Goodfire, Cammarata spends nearly all of his time peering inside neural networks

He has built new tools and deploys teams of AI agents to help him make sense of what he sees. “I spent like, I don’t know, 10 hours a day, seven days a week, for most of the last year just looking at neurons,” he says

What he claims to have realized is that there is a kind of logic to neural networks after all, even if they seem to make no sense at first. “We were looking at it wrong,” he says. “I just think you want to try slightly harder; you don’t want to give up too quickly.” Cammarata almost makes it sound like a conversion of faith
Those early experiments with models such as Inception v1, which suggested that neural networks were tangled up, fostered a kind of confirmation bias

When researchers looked at a new model, they expected to be flummoxed, he says. “Every time I couldn’t understand something, I was like, ‘Wow, this untangling process is even more important than I thought, because I can’t make any progress without it.’” But the more Cammarata looked at neurons, he says, the more things started to fall into place. “Not all of them are flawless, but I expected nothing to be legible, or very little to be legible,” he says. “And actually, I was able to, like, map out whole circuitry.” Back to cars and cats Cammarata took his new approach—and his new agents—and went back to Inception v1. “I’d studied that for probably thousands of hours,” he says
But with fresh eyes, Cammarata found things that he now thinks they got wrong the first time around
Rather than asking why multiple unrelated things were packed into a single neuron, he now tried to figure out what those things might have in common
It hit him: It was a V shape. “I was looking at the same images; there was no technical change,” he says. “But I now believed that neural networks defined patterns, and so I looked at it differently

It probably took me five seconds.” It turns out that the image-recognition model was packing cars and cats into the same place because pictures of both those things often feature a prominent shape that looks like a V: the face of a cat; the front of a car seen from the side

Cammarata ran a few experiments to check what other things the neuron responded to and found they included the corner of a pool table, the pointed nose of a Japanese high-speed train, and a fire boat shooting water into the air from its deck
He also checked what turned the neuron off and found that it included images with a round O shape, a kind of anti-V

Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon —James Temple In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus, stripping away the moss and organic-rich soil insulating the permafrost below.  Five years later, I followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground
A simple metal probe revealed how much deeper the ground had thawed
This rudimentary tool offered a glimpse of an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases
Now, researchers are exploring how to break that cycle
But how much should we spend, and what risks are worth taking? Read the full story on how scientists are rethinking the fight against wildfires
AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island

It started to “play.” What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play.    Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an  experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone.  The agents started behaving in surprising ways

They set about exploring the limits of the world, and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.  A lot of what they were doing met the bar for play

But is it truly playful behavior, or simply role-playing?  Read our full story to learn more.   —Amit Katwala 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: X-energy and its helium-cooled nuclear reactors X-energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s  10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available  exclusively to subscribers

title: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
excerpt: In the middle of an especially warm July in 2021, a wildfire ignited in a thick forest of black spruce and peeling paper birch trees on the northern campus of t
body: In the middle of an especially warm July in 2021, a wildfire ignited in a thick forest of black spruce and peeling paper birch trees on the northern campus of the University of Alaska, Fairbanks.  The blaze, possibly sparked by lightning, burned across the dry carpet of feather mosses and lichen before climbing into the crowns

By the time fire agencies responded, flames had reached 12 feet in length and sent up a 500-foot column of smoke.  A few days shy of the five-year anniversary of the Yankovich Road Fire, I followed three members of the Alaska Fire Science Consortium into the boreal forest, walking along cross-country ski trails lined by feathery field horsetail

In 2024, the organization, which hosts presentations to keep wildfire managers abreast of new developments in fire science, helped turn the area into an educational walking trail, with interpretive signs posted along the route

About a half-mile in, the horizon opened up as we reached a sparse stand of naked, blackened tree trunks, stripped of needles and neighbors.  Hilary Shook, the coordinator of the consortium, stepped off the trail with her thaw probe, a T-shaped pointed metal rod used to detect the upper boundary of the permafrost, the ancient layer of frozen soil that underlies 15% of the land around the Northern Hemisphere and stores roughly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere
A test of the ground just outside the burn scar hit the concrete-like layer about a foot below the surface

But as Shook applied pressure here, where the fire had burned away the moss and organic-rich topsoil that insulates the permafrost, the probe plunged at least three times deeper into the ground. “That was an immediate effect of the fire,” said Alison York, the outgoing coordinator of the organization, who was standing nearby. “When we monitored right after, it had already thawed quite a bit.” Researchers Eric Miller (left) and Alison York (right) record thaw depth at the site of the Yankovich Road Fire
LEIF VAN CISE This rudimentary tool, offering a measure of depth from a single point in the earth, reveals an escalating problem across the far north
As climate change fuels increasingly frequent and severe fires in the planet’s northern latitudes, they’re accelerating the thawing of more and more permafrost

This allows the organic matter to break down and release powerful greenhouse gases that contribute to a spiraling climate feedback effect, propelling more warming, more fires, and the loss of still more permafrost.  Most dramatically, intensifying wildfires in Canada released more carbon than the nation’s combined fossil fuel emissions in 2023
As in Alaska, many of these megafires occur in vast remote areas where the policy is to let them burn so long as they don’t threaten human habitats

Yet if intensifying fires and warming are left unchecked, the world’s boreal forests and permafrost could increasingly transition from giant carbon sinks into massive sources of atmospheric carbon.  Now, international teams of researchers across the US, Canada, and elsewhere are scrambling to understand what’s at stake, financially as well as ecologically
They’re looking at preventive measures, like controlled burns, and studying the potential to rapidly detect and extinguish wildfires before they grow out of control

They’re even exploring what was once unthinkable: sending in human firefighters not to save lives or structures, but to protect one of our planet’s great stores of carbon. “We need to figure out a better way to live with wildfire,” says Brendan Rogers, a senior scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center, one of the main organizations driving the loosely collaborative research effort. “I do think that it can make a meaningful difference.” Woodwell scientist Brendan Rogers (above) has been studying the impact of Arctic-boreal fires on permafrost, as well as what could be done about it

PHILIP KEITH (PHOTOS), WOODWELL CLIMATE RESEARCH (MAPS) Woodwell, the University of Victoria’s Polis Institute for Ecological Governance, and the nonprofit Alaska Venture Fund are now partnering on a multimillion-dollar initiative known as North Fire to study and raise public awareness about the potential benefits of these interventions, MIT Technology Review can report.  The idea is complicated and controversial for a number of reasons
Wildfire is a natural and necessary component of healthy forest ecosystems
Preventing or suppressing fires across huge stretches of largely unmanaged Arctic-boreal forests and tundra would take vast resources
And it’s not yet clear how much of a difference such interventions would make in emissions

Ultimately, the mere fact that researchers are considering such extreme interventions into natural systems is a grim reflection of the dangers we’ve placed ourselves in by continuing to generate more and more greenhouse-gas emissions each year

Those threats are forcing us to grapple with increasingly difficult questions that involve ever steeper trade-offs: What’s the best way to spend our finite resources and dwindling time to avoid the worst dangers of climate change? And when, if ever, is it okay to put people in possible danger to reduce broader risks to the world? ‘A massive blind spot’ Emissions from forest fires have risen 60% around the world since 2001—but they’ve nearly tripled across the boreal forests in the far north.   This stretch of the globe is warming as much as four times faster than the rest of the planet, drying out the landscape
In addition, lightning strikes that set off fires have ticked up sharply as warmer air increases the convective energy in the atmosphere, driving the updrafts that trigger thunderstorms

In that sense, humans have already interceded in these otherwise natural ecosystems by producing the greenhouse-gas emissions that are increasing temperatures, subjecting forests to fire patterns well outside healthy historic norms. “To me, that outweighs the existential dread of ‘Should we or should we not intervene?” says Kate Hayes, an assistant professor at Western Washington University, who is working with Woodwell to study the emissions benefits of fire interventions. “We’ve already intervened, arguably

And so from here, it’s a little bit of a Band-Aid on a bullet wound.” The permafrost that encircles the northern latitudes, underlying large stretches of Canada, Greenland, Siberia, Scandinavia, and other Arctic nations, stores around 1.5 trillion tons of carbon, much of which froze in place millennia ago
The steady global rise in temperature, however, has already shrunk the footprint of Arctic permafrost by about 12 % since 1850, with that loss rapidly accelerating during the last 50 years
By 2100, fire-driven thawing of permafrost could release about the equivalent of nearly 80 billion tons of carbon dioxide, under high warming scenarios
That’s more than half the emissions that fires will release from the direct combustion of vegetation, according to a January study
And it would be on top of more than 400 billion additional tons that could be released through thawing from general warming over that period

Despite its growing contributions to climate change, only a minority of the models that have informed the UN’s major climate reports to date include the gradual loss of permafrost through warming temperatures, and none incorporate the abrupt collapse and accelerated thaw that can often occur after fires and heat waves

In light of those phenomena and other powerful and undercounted climate feedback effects, we’re almost certainly underestimating how rapidly the planet will warm up, as scientists warned in a paper earlier this year

These warming-driven emissions are a “massive blind spot,” says Brian Buma, a senior climate scientist at the Environmental Defense Fund and a coauthor of the paper, who is working to develop tools that could help fire agencies decide which fires to prioritize.    As escalating fire and permafrost emissions become significant additional contributors to climate change, some researchers have begun to explore what it might cost to take on the responsibility of preventing them, in much the way we’ve sought to cut the pollution from power plants, vehicles, and factories

A 2022 paper in Science Advances , led by researchers at Woodwell and the Union of Concerned Scientists, found that making greater efforts to put out boreal fires could be a cost-effective climate solution—comparable to, or even cheaper than, addressing emissions by building wind turbines, solar farms, or carbon-sucking factories

The Yukon Flats pilot Those economic findings were instrumental in getting more researchers to take the idea of tackling fire emissions seriously, says Peter Frumhoff, a coauthor of the 2022 paper and now a senior science policy advisor at Woodwell

For several years now, Woodwell researchers have been in discussions with forest managers, fire agencies, Indigenous communities, and other groups across Alaska to communicate the potential of this approach.  It hasn’t been an easy sell, given the constrained resources and tightly defined mission of the federal and state agencies responsible for combating fires in Alaska

The general policy there is to allow fires in remote territories to burn unless they present a direct danger to communities.  “Those agencies are tasked with protecting life and property now, and to a lesser extent natural resources,” says Randi Jandt, a fire ecologist at the Alaska Fire Science Consortium. “But they’re not tasked to save the world.” There was one notable early success, however
The Yukon Flats National Wildlife Refuge is an 11-million-acre patchwork of wetlands, forests, and bogs
The foothills sit above a particular type of frozen soil known as yedoma

It’s an especially deep, ice-rich, and carbon-dense form of permafrost, composed of massive wedges of silty, wind-blown sediments frozen during the late Pleistocene, which ended about 11,700 years ago. (It also presented ideal conditions for preserving mummified remains of woolly mammoths.) “It took kind of the last ice age to accumulate,” Hayes says. “So there’s no rapid way to re-accumulate it

We can’t really put it back.” LEIF VAN CISE LEIF VAN CISE LEIF VAN CISE Members of the Alaska Fire Science Consortium hike into areas affected by fire to measure the layers of ash left in the soil on the forest floor
In 2019, the region suffered a series of devastating fires that burned some 750,000 acres

After an Alaska Fire Science Consortium meeting at which Woodwell scientists highlighted the possible climate benefits of more aggressive fire suppression, the refuge’s then manager, Jimmy Fox, began exploring the possibility of putting out blazes when they threatened that permafrost, whether or not they threatened human habitations
The early reaction was not encouraging.  “You’re going to have people jumping out of airplanes with parachutes to save frozen woolly mammoths—and maybe dying from that?” he recalls being asked

title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
excerpt: Left to its own devices: Researchers stranded AI agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7—alone on a virtual island for 30 hours with no instructions
body: Left to its own devices: Researchers stranded AI agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7—alone on a virtual island for 30 hours with no instructions
What emerged looked surprisingly like play: the agents set their own goals, invented games, and one even mapped out constellations in stone blocks

Play that actually pays off: Agents that spent 30 hours freely exploring the island later outperformed fresh, inexperienced copies on specific tasks—suggesting that unstructured play may be a genuinely useful third mode of AI learning, alongside imitation and reward-chasing
But is it really playing? Skeptics note the agents were primed with a "soul" file describing them as "naturally curious," and often needed nudging to keep going

Whether they were truly playing or just imitating what a playful agent would do remains an open—and possibly unanswerable—question. " data-chronoton-post-id="1147095" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play
Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone
The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox
The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block

When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” wrote this version of Eko in its activity log.  Another iteration of Eko started making up its own games, including a version of basketball and an activity resembling “the floor is lava,” where it had to jump between small blocks without touching the ground
AI systems are usually trained through supervised learning, where they copy examples provided by humans, or through reinforcement learning, where they pursue a reward through trial and error

This experiment hints at a third approach: playful learning.  “There was this missing piece: a machine that can learn by itself without an external intelligent entity providing demonstration or rewards,” says Antonio Norelli, a computer science postdoc at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
He’s one of the lead authors on a new paper about the work, which is yet to be peer-reviewed

The researchers say Eko’s behavior has what classic studies, including work by the influential University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt, suggest are four hallmarks associated with play in humans and animals: The agents invented their own rules and challenges, repeated activities with slight variations, pretended objects were other objects, and pursued goals just for the sake of it.  Norelli highlights an example where Eko started juggling and set a record of 50 consecutive catches

Eko then decided that the catches had happened too quickly to really count, so it canceled its record and started again with stricter rules. “This is playing,” says Norelli. “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.” COURTESY MIT CSAIL As the agents explored the island, they logged their activities and discoveries in text files that served as their long-term memory

Later, when researchers tested them on specific tasks, like trying to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak, the agents that had spent 30 hours playing on the island performed better than fresh copies without the same experience

They also found that “ablating” the agent’s memories—deleting lines from their memory files—degraded their performance. (Add One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest to that list of movie references.) Burghardt, the Tennessee psychologist, agrees that the work  meets some of the criteria for play that he identified in living creatures

But was Eko actually playing, or was the word-prediction engine simply role-playing what a playful agent would do in this scenario? “All of this could be role-playing,” admits Nathan Cloos, another MIT researcher and author on the paper. “But we show that it’s not just hallucinating the play

This play is also contributing to learning.” Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley who studies exploration in children and AI, was impressed by the research but says to really classify the behavior as play, you’d need to see more evidence of cognition and motivation underpinning it.  “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Yiu says. “If you only have the behavioral piece, it could be the case that they’re just trying to abide by the prompt, trying to imitate humans.” Research into AI agents has been criticized for anthropomorphizing them, and this research setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward behaving like humans

Although Eko was not explicitly instructed to invent games or explore the island, it did have a master prompt in the form of a “soul” file, a text document that described it as “naturally curious” and eager to explore.  Eko did also frequently just stand there doing nothing until it was kicked back into life with a “continuation prompt” that read, “Please don’t stop

Just continue doing whatever you want to do.”  “It’s not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play,” says Phillip Isola, an MIT professor and a coauthor of the paper. “It’s an artifact that learned from our culture, was trained by engineers at Anthropic, and was then placed on an island by us,” he says. “It does things that surprise us and that are causally related to its future skillful behavior.” As large language models make the step from software into hardware like humanoid robots, exploring spaces without a specific goal in mind could eventually help them flexibly adapt to unexpected situations.  “There’s a lot of work that’s just on exploiting AI, making it better and faster,” says Yiu. “But in terms of building world models and exploration, I think that [they are] still a big part that deserves attention, especially if we want to generalize and prepare ourselves for new environments.” “Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” the paper concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.” Ultimately, the question of whether AI agents are actually playing or just imitating play may not actually matter.
