title: How far can we push computing?
excerpt: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next
body: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next

On the evening of December 29, 1959, at an American Physical Society meeting at Caltech, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom,” on how we might manipulate and control things on an extremely small scale

There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued, or from storing every book ever written in something the size of a dust speck—or, ultimately, from arranging matter atom by atom
Biology already did versions of this (a living cell keeps its instructions in a wisp of DNA), so all of this was plainly permitted by the laws of physics
In other words, there was plenty of room at the bottom
He was right, and for decades we descended into that space almost for free
The transistor—the switch at the heart of computer chips—repeatedly halved in size so that chips doubled in density; a computer that once filled a room now fits inside a watch
But that easy descent has now stalled, and the clearest sign is the buildout of data centers

Six of the biggest hyperscalers, the companies that run the world’s largest such facilities, are on track to spend more than $700 billion this year on computing infrastructure, about twice the record they set in 2025, pouring concrete and copper and silicon into new sites faster than the electrical grid can feed them
That buildout buys performance by brute force, adding more of what we already know how to make
The other kind of progress, the kind that made computer chips better, is the one that is quietly running out
The trend lines that tracked the dramatic improvements of the 20th-century information age are now bending—or breaking—with the dawn of the 21st century’s intelligence age

Moore’s Law, which plots how densely transistors can be constructed on silicon, has slowed down; Dennard’s Law, which states that power consumption in a given patch of computer chip stays the same even as it gets more and more packed with smaller and smaller transistors, has ended; Koomey’s Law, which traces how much computation we can wring from each joule of energy, has begun to flag; Kryder’s Law, which describes how tightly bits can be packed to build magnetic storage, has slowed to a crawl; and Keck’s Law, which charts the exponential rise in the amount of information a single conventional optical fiber can carry, is flattening.  But these scaling laws are merely observations about systems that we have engineered; they are not fundamental physical laws
The physical limits of computing and communications—dictated by quantum mechanics, general relativity, and information theory—lie far below anything in a data center today
The scaling laws chart the descent behind us
The fundamental physical limits chart the room that remains
Some of these limits may be far out of reach in practice
But they are still worth exploring, because the work pays twice: once in technology development and once in fundamental science

A proof-of-­concept system that approaches a limit is at once a technology that forces stalled paradigms to give way and an experiment that deepens our understanding of the physical laws themselves.  The descent During his 1959 lecture, Feynman offered two prizes of $1,000 each out of his own pocket
One would go to the first person to build a working electric motor smaller than a 0.4-millimeter cube
He expected the challenge to force someone to invent a genuinely new microtechnology
Instead, about a year later, a Caltech-trained engineer named William McLellan turned up with the motor built and running
The ­quarter-­milligram machine, roughly the size of a grain of sand, had been assembled by hand with a toothpick and a watch­maker’s lathe, under a microscope
Feynman, by his own account, was only slightly disappointed
The prize had proved his point in the least interesting way imaginable
The room really was down there, but reaching this first milestone had taken no new technology at all—just an unusually patient man with steady hands
The second prize aged differently, and more instructively
It was offered to whoever could shrink a page of text by a factor of 25,000 in each direction, small enough for the whole Britannica to fit on a pinhead
That one stood unclaimed for a quarter of a century

It was finally won in 1985 by Tom Newman, a Stanford graduate student who used an electron-beam lithography machine—an ancestor of pattern-making tools used in chipmaking today—to transcribe the opening page of A Tale of Two Cities at the required scale
The descent was already well underway, however

The year before Feynman’s talk, Jack Kilby, newly hired at Texas Instruments and with no vacation yet to take, spent that July nearly alone in the lab while his colleagues enjoyed time off, and by that September he had wired together a transistor, a capacitor, and three resistors, all made from a single sliver of germanium

This proved that an entire circuit could be carved from one block of semiconductor.  The machine, roughly the size of a grain of sand, had been assembled by hand with a toothpick and a watch­maker’s lathe, under a microscope

The idea took off, and the number of components on a chip kept doubling on a schedule so regular that Gordon Moore, in a 1965 trade-magazine article, simply drew a line through the trend and extended it into the future
Moore, though, never claimed transistors could shrink forever
He observed that at any given moment there is a certain number of components that makes each one of them as cheap as possible to manufacture
Put in too few transistors and you waste the chip; cram in too many and manufacturing errors multiply and yields collapse

It was this cost-minimizing number that was doubling at a steady pace.  For four decades the descent came with another gift: Dennard scaling, so named for the IBM engineer Robert Dennard, who spelled it out in 1974
Each time transistors shrank, they also switched faster and drew proportionally less power, so every generation was an automatic win

Chips could no longer shed the heat of running every transistor flat out; clock speeds, which had raced past three gigahertz, stopped climbing, and Intel canceled the four-gigahertz processor it had promised

title: Many vapes and e-cigarettes are now banned in Pennsylvania – here’s what Philly consumers and businesses need to know
url:
<title>Many vapes and e-cigarettes are now banned in Pennsylvania – here’s what Philly consumers and businesses need to know</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767049/original/file-20261019-50-8arb3c.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6650%2C4433&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The new law allows Pennsylvania businesses to sell products from just six vape manufacturers, but that list includes some of the most popular brands.
</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Vaping%20Change%20FDA/40b9a901164945188c0020d27c5914d0/photo">AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Many popular nicotine vapes are now <a href="https://www.inquirer.com/news/pennsylvania/pennsylvania-vape-ban-list-20261008.html">banned in Pennsylvania</a>, with only six companies approved to sell their products in the state after a legal ban went into effect on Oct. 19, 2026.</p>

<p>I am a <a href="https://www.villanova.edu/university/law/faculty-scholarship/faculty-directory/profiles/AnaSantosRutschman.html">health law professor</a> at Villanova University outside Philadelphia. </p>

<p>Here’s how Pennsylvania’s new law works and what to expect as enforcement begins – especially in Philadelphia, where proximity to states with different laws might pose some challenges.</p>

<h2>Banned products</h2>

<p>The products in question include e-cigarettes, vapes and other electronic nicotine delivery systems, commonly known as <a href="https://www.fda.gov/tobacco-products/tobacco-products-ingredients-components/e-cigarettes-vapes-and-other-electronic-nicotine-delivery-systems-ends">ENDS</a>. </p>

<p>These products dispense an inhalable aerosol that <a href="https://cancercontrol.cancer.gov/brp/tcrb/electronic-nicotine-delivery-systems">contains nicotine and other chemicals</a>, including flavoring agents.</p>

<p>ENDS are the <a href="https://www.doi.org/10.1016/j.cppeds.2020.100761">most common form of tobacco used by teens and young adults</a>. Flavored vapes are <a href="https://www.doi.org/10.1016/j.addbeh.2020.106773">especially appealing</a> to <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco/e-cigarettes/why-youth-vape.html">middle and high school students</a>.</p>

<p>In recent years, a growing body of research has studied the <a href="https://www.doi.org/10.1007/s10552-020-01307-y">health impact of ENDS</a> use, particularly among younger smokers. These studies have raised concerns not only about long-term addiction to nicotine but also <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco/e-cigarettes/health-effects.html">exposure to potentially carcinogenic</a> or otherwise harmful chemicals. In 2018, the <a href="https://www.hhs.gov/surgeongeneral/reports-and-publications/youth-vaping/index.html">U.S. surgeon general declared</a> youth vaping an epidemic.</p>

<p>At the federal level, ENDS are <a href="https://www.fda.gov/tobacco-products/market-and-distribute-tobacco-product/e-cigarettes-vapes-and-other-electronic-nicotine-delivery-systems-ends-authorized-fda">regulated by the Food and Drug Administration</a>, but states have the authority to restrict their sale in order to protect the health of their citizens. This is precisely what Pennsylvania has done, <a href="https://www.publichealthlawcenter.org/resources/state-e-cigarette-registry-bill-map">joining more than a dozen other states</a> with similar registry laws.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Woman sits on couch and vapes" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767043/original/file-20261019-50-blvelg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C451%2C8640%2C4860&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767043/original/file-20261019-50-blvelg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767043/original/file-20261019-50-blvelg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767043/original/file-20261019-50-blvelg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767043/original/file-20261019-50-blvelg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767043/original/file-20261019-50-blvelg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767043/original/file-20261019-50-blvelg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Vapes dispense an inhalable aerosol that contains nicotine and other chemicals, including flavoring agents.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/woman-at-home-vaping-royalty-free-image/1475425958">E+ Collection/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Some popular brands can still be sold</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://www.attorneygeneral.gov/wp-content/uploads/Act-No-57-for-2025.pdf">new law</a> requires the state attorney general to maintain a registry of ENDS approved for sale in Pennsylvania. If a product is not listed in the <a href="https://www.attorneygeneral.gov/businesses-and-organizations/electronic-nicotine-delivery-system-laws-forms-directory/">directory</a>, businesses that sell them will face fines.</p>

<p>The directory currently includes <a href="https://www.attorneygeneral.gov/businesses-and-organizations/electronic-nicotine-delivery-system-laws-forms-directory/ends-directory/">products from just six manufacturers</a>: Juul Labs, R.J. Reynolds Vapor Co., Blue Nine, Custom Technologies, NJoy and Schwartz E-Liquid. However, these manufacturers produce several of the <a href="https://tobaccomonitoring.org/national/">most well-known brands of ENDS</a>, and many of the products included in the directory are <a href="https://www.inquirer.com/news/pennsylvania/pennsylvania-vape-ban-list-20261008.html">extremely popular</a>, such as Juul vaporizers. The reason the new law <a href="https://www.attorneygeneral.gov/wp-content/uploads/Act-No-57-for-2025.pdf">allows these specific products</a> to continue to be sold is that they have been evaluated by the FDA. </p>

<p>The directory does exclude some very <a href="https://tobaccomonitoring.org/national/">popular</a> products as well, including many brands of disposable vapes and vape juice. The law was designed to specifically ban products that have not been evaluated by the FDA.</p>

<h2>Penalties for businesses</h2>

<p>If a business sells or offers to sell a product that is not in the directory, the <a href="https://www.attorneygeneral.gov/wp-content/uploads/Act-No-57-for-2025.pdf">consequences can be severe</a>. </p>

<p>For first-time violations, there will be a fine of up to US$500 per product. A second violation within a year will trigger a fine of $1,000 per day per product until the product is either removed or appears listed in the directory. It will also lead to suspension of the license to sell tobacco products for at least 14 days. A third violation within a year will raise the fine to $1,500 per day per product, coupled with license revocation.</p>

<p>Attorney General David Sunday says his office will focus on “<a href="https://www.attorneygeneral.gov/taking-action/enforcement-of-act-57-which-prohibits-pa-sales-of-unapproved-vape-and-e-cigarette-products-can-begin-october-19/">targeted enforcement</a>.” What exactly targeted enforcement means is unclear, but the new law authorizes unannounced inspections. In addition to the premises, inspectors can also <a href="https://www.attorneygeneral.gov/wp-content/uploads/Act-No-57-for-2025.pdf">examine books and records</a>.</p>

<p>Illegal products that are offered for sale will be <a href="https://www.attorneygeneral.gov/wp-content/uploads/Act-No-57-for-2025.pdf">subject to seizure and forfeiture</a>, as well as destruction at the business’s expense.</p>

<p>The new law does not impose penalties on consumers who purchase banned products. </p>

<h2>What to expect in Philadelphia</h2>

<p>Philadelphia was an early adopter of a restrictive approach to the sale of vaping products due to concerns about the youth vaping epidemic. In 2019 the city <a href="https://www.phila.gov/2019-12-19-mayor-signs-laws-restricting-e-cigs-and-banning-flavored-cigarillos/">banned the sale</a> of certain flavored ENDS that were especially popular among <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco/e-cigarettes/why-youth-vape.html">adolescent and teen smokers</a>. </p>

<p>Pennsylvania as a whole, however, has been <a href="https://www.fox29.com/news/nicotine-vape-laws-across-northeast-what-you-need-know-2026">less assertive than some of its neighbors</a>, <a href="https://casaa.org/get-involved/state-locator/new-york/">such as New York</a>, in trying to stop youth vaping. The American Lung Association rates Pennsylvania in the <a href="https://www.lung.org/research/sotc/state-grades/pennsylvania">D to F range</a> for its tobacco control policies, below nearby New Jersey, New York and Delaware.</p>

<p>While the Pennsylvania law will reduce the number of products that can be legally sold in the state, it will still be relatively easy for a consumer in Philadelphia to travel to New Jersey or Delaware and buy some of the products banned under Pennsylvania law, including popular brands of disposable vapes. </p>

<p>But additional tobacco control measures may be underway, especially in Philadelphia. On Oct. 15 a member of the Philadelphia City Council <a href="https://www.nbcphiladelphia.com/news/local/philadelphia-councilmember-proposes-new-restrictions-on-where-smoke-shops-can-open/4479385/">introduced a bill</a> that would amend zoning laws in a way that would effectively <a href="https://www.inquirer.com/politics/philadelphia/city-council-smoke-shops-shane-seiber-20261015.html">prevent new businesses selling tobacco and vaping products</a> from opening in many areas of the city.</p>

body: The new law allows Pennsylvania businesses to sell products from just six vape manufacturers, but that list includes some of the most popular brands

AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell Many popular nicotine vapes are now banned in Pennsylvania , with only six companies approved to sell their products in the state after a legal ban went into effect on Oct. 19, 2026
I am a health law professor at Villanova University outside Philadelphia
Here’s how Pennsylvania’s new law works and what to expect as enforcement begins – especially in Philadelphia, where proximity to states with different laws might pose some challenges
Banned products The products in question include e-cigarettes, vapes and other electronic nicotine delivery systems, commonly known as ENDS
These products dispense an inhalable aerosol that contains nicotine and other chemicals , including flavoring agents
ENDS are the most common form of tobacco used by teens and young adults
Flavored vapes are especially appealing to middle and high school students
In recent years, a growing body of research has studied the health impact of ENDS use, particularly among younger smokers
These studies have raised concerns not only about long-term addiction to nicotine but also exposure to potentially carcinogenic or otherwise harmful chemicals
In 2018, the U.S. surgeon general declared youth vaping an epidemic
At the federal level, ENDS are regulated by the Food and Drug Administration , but states have the authority to restrict their sale in order to protect the health of their citizens
This is precisely what Pennsylvania has done, joining more than a dozen other states with similar registry laws
Vapes dispense an inhalable aerosol that contains nicotine and other chemicals, including flavoring agents
E+ Collection/Getty Images Some popular brands can still be sold The new law requires the state attorney general to maintain a registry of ENDS approved for sale in Pennsylvania
If a product is not listed in the directory , businesses that sell them will face fines
The directory currently includes products from just six manufacturers : Juul Labs, R.J
Reynolds Vapor Co., Blue Nine, Custom Technologies, NJoy and Schwartz E-Liquid
However, these manufacturers produce several of the most well-known brands of ENDS , and many of the products included in the directory are extremely popular , such as Juul vaporizers
The reason the new law allows these specific products to continue to be sold is that they have been evaluated by the FDA
The directory does exclude some very popular products as well, including many brands of disposable vapes and vape juice
The law was designed to specifically ban products that have not been evaluated by the FDA
Penalties for businesses If a business sells or offers to sell a product that is not in the directory, the consequences can be severe
For first-time violations, there will be a fine of up to US$500 per product
A second violation within a year will trigger a fine of $1,000 per day per product until the product is either removed or appears listed in the directory
It will also lead to suspension of the license to sell tobacco products for at least 14 days
A third violation within a year will raise the fine to $1,500 per day per product, coupled with license revocation
Attorney General David Sunday says his office will focus on “ targeted enforcement .” What exactly targeted enforcement means is unclear, but the new law authorizes unannounced inspections
In addition to the premises, inspectors can also examine books and records
Illegal products that are offered for sale will be subject to seizure and forfeiture , as well as destruction at the business’s expense
The new law does not impose penalties on consumers who purchase banned products
What to expect in Philadelphia Philadelphia was an early adopter of a restrictive approach to the sale of vaping products due to concerns about the youth vaping epidemic
In 2019 the city banned the sale of certain flavored ENDS that were especially popular among adolescent and teen smokers
Pennsylvania as a whole, however, has been less assertive than some of its neighbors , such as New York , in trying to stop youth vaping
The American Lung Association rates Pennsylvania in the D to F range for its tobacco control policies, below nearby New Jersey, New York and Delaware

While the Pennsylvania law will reduce the number of products that can be legally sold in the state, it will still be relatively easy for a consumer in Philadelphia to travel to New Jersey or Delaware and buy some of the products banned under Pennsylvania law, including popular brands of disposable vapes
But additional tobacco control measures may be underway, especially in Philadelphia

On Oct. 15 a member of the Philadelphia City Council introduced a bill that would amend zoning laws in a way that would effectively prevent new businesses selling tobacco and vaping products from opening in many areas of the city

<title>Federal spending on climate change before 2024 election boosted incumbents of both parties</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765629/original/file-20261012-50-sumrqk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5953%2C3968&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The U.S. House of Representatives votes on the Inflation Reduction Act in August 2022.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/CongressBudget/5aeabed2cd4541549de09d81aadc1d6f/photo">AP Photo/Patrick Semansky</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>A massive federal spending effort to combat climate change passed in 2022 without a single Republican vote <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/117th-congress/house-bill/5376/actions">in the U.S. House</a> <a href="https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1172/vote_117_2_00325.htm#position">or the Senate</a>. But the billions of dollars it authorized <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s44168-026-00402-1">benefited Republican and Democratic politicians alike</a> – so long as they were already in the House of Representatives – according to an analysis I conducted with several fellow researchers. The results suggest that incumbents can still reap electoral rewards when federal money reaches their districts, even if they opposed the bill that provided it.</p>

<p>Enacted in 2022, the <a href="https://www.wri.org/update/brief-summary-climate-and-energy-provisions-inflation-reduction-act-2022">Inflation Reduction Act</a> <a href="https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1172/vote_117_2_00325.htm#position">squeaked through the Senate</a> only through a <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Tie-breaking_votes_cast_by_Kamala_Harris_in_the_U.S._Senate">tiebreaking vote cast by Vice President Kamala Harris</a>. It authorized spending <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2022/08/16/business/biden-climate-tax-inflation-reduction.html">US$370 billion to combat climate change and lower greenhouse gas emissions</a>, primarily through subsidies such as a <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/IN/PDF/IN11996/IN11996.3.pdf">tax credit of up to $7,500</a> for buying an electric vehicle and incentives for making <a href="https://www.irs.gov/credits-deductions/energy-efficient-commercial-buildings-deduction">commercial buildings more energy efficient</a>, rather than by imposing new fees or taxes.</p>

<p>Before the 2024 election, over <a href="https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/99QB8Q">$204 billion</a> had been spent on clean energy projects around the country, through a combination of private investment and federal incentives.</p>

<p>While Republicans opposed the legislation, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s44168-026-00402-1">79% of the law’s investment</a> went to Republican congressional districts.</p>

<p>Even when Republicans vote against climate legislation at the national level, at least some favor <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-022-03335-w">investing in clean energy technology</a> at the state and local level, because those investments bring local economic benefits. Many Republican districts, which are often large and more rural, are well suited to these kinds of projects.</p>

<p><iframe id="FNLWQ" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/FNLWQ/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A map of the U.S. showing amounts of money spent in each congressional district under the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022."></iframe></p>

<h2>Benefits of federal investment</h2>

<p>Elected officials are sometimes accused of “<a href="https://www.investopedia.com/ask/answers/050615/where-did-phrase-pork-barrel-come.asp">pork barrel politics</a>,” seeking to direct federal taxpayer spending to their own congressional districts. In part that’s because voters see federal investment as creating local jobs and stimulating economic growth.</p>

<p>Although no Republican voted for the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, some Republican lawmakers began defending parts of the law as investments reached their districts. In August 2024, heading into the election, <a href="https://garbarino.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/garbarino.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/FINAL%20Credits%20Letter%202024.08.06.pdf">18 Republican House members urged</a> House Speaker Mike Johnson to preserve the law’s clean energy tax credits, which they said “created good jobs in many parts of the country – including many districts represented by members of our conference.” </p>

<p>That support continued after the election. In March 2025, after Republicans retained control of the House and party leaders began considering cuts to the law’s programs, even <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2025/03/10/house-republican-clean-energy-tax-breaks-00218126">more Republican House members called</a> for preserving the clean energy tax credits, which could be used, for example, to finance a large wind energy project or construction of a battery factory. The lawmakers argued that repealing the credits while major projects were still under construction would jeopardize investments already underway and the jobs tied to them.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765649/original/file-20261012-50-ortryl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A large building is under construction, with many trucks and other pieces of equipment outside." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765649/original/file-20261012-50-ortryl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765649/original/file-20261012-50-ortryl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765649/original/file-20261012-50-ortryl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765649/original/file-20261012-50-ortryl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765649/original/file-20261012-50-ortryl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765649/original/file-20261012-50-ortryl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765649/original/file-20261012-50-ortryl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A Toyota battery-manufacturing plant in Liberty, N.C., received billions in support through the Inflation Reduction Act.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/the-exterior-of-the-new-toyota-battery-manufacturing-news-photo/2147745172">Logan Cyrus/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The bill’s funding affected the 2024 election</h2>

<p>Our analysis finds that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s44168-026-00402-1">Inflation Reduction Act funding helped incumbent House members</a> of both parties in the 2024 election. </p>

<p>During the campaign, both Democrats and Republicans highlighted benefits of the investments funded by the act. Republicans usually used language like “<a href="https://rollcall.com/2024/10/28/vulnerable-candidates-get-creative-as-they-vie-for-climate-votes/">economic development opportunities</a>,” while Democrats <a href="https://x.com/BillPascrell/status/1805990411338752222">directly mentioned</a> the act itself.</p>

<p>Some districts got nothing, and one got nearly $8 billion. Some of the largest investments were in Republican-held districts in <a href="https://www.wardsauto.com/news/archive-auto-toyota-begins-production-expanded-north-carolina-plant/739375/">North Carolina</a> and <a href="https://apnews.com/article/hyundai-ev-georgia-production-begins-ioniq-424cf322822f707e7070260a789ffb59">Georgia</a> to expand capacity at electric vehicle plants already under construction. These companies were eligible for <a href="https://www.irs.gov/credits-and-deductions-under-the-inflation-reduction-act-of-2022">corporate tax breaks</a> from the law and hoped to benefit from <a href="https://www.eenews.net/articles/reality-of-repealing-green-credits-sinks-in-for-divided-gop/">increased consumer demand</a> because of the law’s tax credit for people purchasing electric vehicles.</p>

<p>In Mississippi’s 2nd Congressional District, which got $588 million in funding from the Inflation Reduction Act, Rep. Bennie Thompson, a Democrat, received 61.8% of the vote in 2024, up from 60% in 2022. In Michigan’s 5th District, which got almost $2 billion under the law, Rep. Tim Walberg, a Republican, received 65.7% of the vote in 2024, up from 62% in 2022.</p>

<p>We found that the more money a representative’s district got from the Inflation Reduction Act, the more the candidate improved their electoral performance in 2024 over how they had done in 2022. </p>

<p>When we conducted our statistical analysis, we accounted for multiple factors that could influence election results, including the district’s support for Trump, the incumbent’s previous vote share, campaign spending and district demographics. Using <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-does-it-mean-to-control-for-variables-in-a-scientific-study-a-statistician-explains-287456">statistical methods to isolate the effects</a> of Inflation Reduction Act funding, we found that doubling the amount of federal investment in a congressional district led to about a 0.9 percentage-point increase in the incumbent’s 2024 vote share relative to their 2022 result.</p>

<p>Our analysis showed that both Democratic and Republican incumbents saw electoral benefits from Inflation Reduction Act investment, even though Republicans in Congress had universally opposed the legislation. While some incumbents still lost votes or their seats, the data showed that greater Inflation Reduction Act investment helped them perform better than they otherwise would have.</p>

<p>These results indicate that voters may respond more to the money coming into their districts than to the underlying purpose of that funding.</p>

<p>While previous federal spending projects helped <a href="https://doi.org/10.1086/262064">incumbent House members in elections</a>, we found no direct evidence that district economies improved between 2022 and 2024. Instead, it’s more likely that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/lsq.12425">incumbents claiming credit</a> for the  investments on the campaign trail explained why election results improved with Inflation Reduction Act funding. The lesson is that voters pay attention to actual or promised investments that might come into their areas.</p>

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">President Donald Trump signs a major tax cut and spending cut bill on July 4, 2025.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/president-donald-trump-joined-by-republican-lawmakers-signs-news-photo/2223602542">Samuel Corum/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Dismantling the subsidies and tax breaks</h2>

<p>Upon taking office in 2025, the Trump administration and the Republican majority in the House <a href="https://time.com/7258269/trump-climate-policies-executive-orders/">rolled back many of the law’s climate provisions</a>. A massive package of tax breaks and spending cuts sometimes referred to as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” <a href="https://www.cfr.org/articles/congresss-one-big-beautiful-bill-will-shrink-renewable-energy-investments-yet-some">removed tax credits for energy efficiency improvements</a> and electric vehicle purchases. </p>

<p>The Trump administration has also moved to <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/02/american-energy-dominance-is-back-under-president-trump/">expand fossil fuel production</a> on federal lands.</p>

<p>This evidence indicates that presidential priorities can outweigh even direct benefits to House members on highly polarized issues. The fact that <a href="https://www.bluegreenalliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/OBBBA-user-guide.pdf">some climate-related tax credits remained</a> even after passage of the big budget bill does indicate that economic development policies may remain appealing to Republican leadership.</p>

<p>These electoral benefits indicate voters may reward investments even when the policies that created them remain politically contentious. Economic investments in fighting climate change can generate local political benefits across party lines, even if those benefits are not enough to overcome national divisions over climate change.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293791/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>A pregnant mom let her 5-year-old stay outside to collect goose feathers – and was placed on the child abuse and neglect registry</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766748/original/file-20261016-72-al6s1i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=963%2C0%2C3287%2C2191&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">If you take your eyes off your 5-year-old son, are you promoting his independence or putting him in danger?</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/piece-of-nature-royalty-free-image/168270396?phrase=kid%20holding%20goose%20feather&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Adriana Varela Photography/Moment via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Ford’s Colony in Williamsburg <a href="https://fordscolonyliving.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/Welcome-Brochure-2021-08-2021.pdf">is a leafy, gated community</a> in Virginia’s colonial-era historic region with 10 miles of trails and 24-hour security. </p>

<p>On June 5, 2026, Karyann Parkinson, a recent law school graduate pregnant with her fifth child, was on a walk through their neighborhood in Ford’s Colony with her 5-year-old son. On their way home, her son asked if he <a href="https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/parenting/article/arrested-five-year-old-walk-alone-77cksxhzd">could collect a few goose feathers</a> at a nearby pond. She said yes, confident in his ability to walk there and back safely. </p>

<p>About 20 minutes later, a security guard from Ford’s Colony knocked on her door, with her son by his side. He explained that a neighbor had seen the child walking by himself, and that he was going to call the police to report her. Within an hour, law enforcement and child protective services were at Parkinson’s door to inform her that they were <a href="https://www.pilotonline.com/2026/09/12/james-city-county-mom-son-walk-alone/">investigating her for neglect</a>. </p>

<p>After being placed on the child abuse and neglect registry for <a href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/virginia-mom-gets-6-month-113005821.html">lack of supervision</a>, Parkinson was convicted of contributing to the delinquency of a minor and received a six-month suspended jail sentence. Parkinson has appealed to the Circuit Court and will have a <a href="https://www.thefp.com/p/she-let-her-son-go-walk-convicted-criminal-regulation-parenting-choice">jury trial</a> in 2027.</p>

<p>I stumbled upon Parkinson’s case while researching and writing a law review article about states that are trying to encourage childhood independence by lessening penalties on parents who allow their children to play outdoors while unsupervised. 
Virginia, ironically, is one of those states.</p>

<p>Parkinson’s experience is not unique. <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=BnKXttEAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">In my scholarship</a> and in my work as a family lawyer, I’ve seen how overly broad child neglect laws can fail families. </p>

<p>These statutes are being revisited as <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2024/09/15/opinion/parenting-helicopter-ignoring.html">scholars</a>, <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/authors/271851/peter-gray/">psychologists</a> <a href="https://www.freerangekids.com/">and journalists</a> are increasingly finding fault with “helicopter parenting,” or overprotective parenting that limits children’s independence and autonomy.</p>

<p>Yet cases like Parkinson’s suggest that when the boundaries of neglect are unclear, the law continues to give parents a powerful incentive to err on the side of constant supervision.</p>

<h2>Vague language casts a wide net</h2>

<p>In 1974, Congress passed <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/93rd-congress/senate-bill/1191">the Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act</a> to promote child safety and improve how child welfare services are provided. </p>

<p>The law <a href="https://acf.gov/cb/grants-funding/child-abuse-prevention-and-treatment-act-capta-state-grants">provides federal funding</a> to states to improve child protective services systems. It also <a href="https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2011-title42/pdf/USCODE-2011-title42-chap67-subchapI-sec5106a.pdf">requires states</a> to have procedures for reporting instances of child abuse and neglect.</p>

<p>To obtain federal funding, states must comply with certain investigative procedures and reporting guidelines. </p>

<p>However, states enact their own laws on child abuse and neglect, each of which includes its own definitions and procedures, such as determining who must report suspected abuse or neglect.</p>

<p>In an effort to ensure instances of true neglect don’t fall through the cracks, state laws typically use vague language. Tennessee, for example, <a href="https://carat.app.tn.gov/carat/pdf/tnchild-37-1-102.pdf">describes a neglected child</a> as “under unlawful or improper care,” while Mississippi law <a href="https://www.mdcps.ms.gov/programs/child-abuse-prevention/legal-definitions-reporting-abuse-and-neglect">categorizes a child as neglected</a> if they are without “proper care, custody, supervision, or support.” </p>

<p>This is how a child whose mom has determined he’s mature enough to collect goose feathers on his own ends up being drawn into the system: An agency could argue that she wasn’t properly supervising him.</p>

<h2>The Parkinson family is not alone</h2>

<p>Other investigations of mothers for child neglect under similar circumstances have regularly cropped up over the past 20 years.</p>

<p>In 2013, an Illinois mother named Natasha Felix let her 11-, 9- and 5-year-old children play in the park adjacent to their home. Even though she could see them from the window, the state determined she met the definition of neglect due to inadequate supervision, <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/mother-cleared-of-neglect-for-letting-kids-play-outside-alone/">a finding that was later reversed</a>.</p>

<p>In 2014, a <a href="https://www.theatlantic.com/national/archive/2014/07/arrested-for-letting-a-9-year-old-play-at-the-park-alone/374436/">South Carolina mother</a>, Debra Harrell, was working at a McDonald’s while her daughter was on summer vacation. During her shift, she allowed her 9-year-old daughter to play at a park about a mile away, giving her a cellphone in case she needed to get in touch. <a href="https://abc7.com/post/mom-faces-felony-charge-for-letting-girl-play-in-park/225384/">Harrell was arrested</a> for felony child neglect, spent 17 days in jail and temporarily lost custody of her daughter. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A young woman pictured from the back gazing out a window with open blinds." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766749/original/file-20261016-50-t52wry.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766749/original/file-20261016-50-t52wry.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766749/original/file-20261016-50-t52wry.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766749/original/file-20261016-50-t52wry.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766749/original/file-20261016-50-t52wry.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766749/original/file-20261016-50-t52wry.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766749/original/file-20261016-50-t52wry.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

<p>A <a href="https://abc7ny.com/post/brittany-patterson-georgia-mom-arrested-after-son-was-reported-walking-alone/15548906/">Georgia mother</a>, Brittany Patterson, was investigated in 2024 because her 10-year-old son had taken a walk to a scenic mountain hamlet called Mineral Bluff, which was about a mile from his home. A woman saw him walking on the road and called the police. Law enforcement arrested the mother for reckless conduct. The charges <a href="https://www.wsbtv.com/news/local/charges-dismissed-north-ga-mom-arrested-when-son-walked-store-alone/QTIJ34BF4NBOPIB3QUMMUQZIMM/">were ultimately dismissed in 2025</a>.</p>

<h2>Parents put in the middle</h2>

<p>Laws may encourage parents to be overprotective, but parenting research is recommending the opposite. </p>

<p>A 2020 study found that kids set free to roam on their own feel <a href="https://theconversation.com/kids-set-free-to-roam-on-their-own-feel-more-confident-navigating-in-adulthood-163972">more confident navigating new places in adulthood</a>. And other research has found that permissive parenting styles – the kind that can give kids opportunities to take risks, whether it’s climbing a tall structure on the playground or exploring the woods behind their house – <a href="https://theconversation.com/denmarks-hands-off-approach-to-parenting-could-offer-a-blueprint-for-raising-more-resilient-self-reliant-kids-281485">help kids learn how to tolerate failure, distress and uncertainty</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/21594937.2022.2152531">and ultimately develop into more competent adults</a>.</p>

<p>That may explain why, in 2018, Utah <a href="https://le.utah.gov/%7E2018/bills/static/SB0065.html">amended its neglect statute</a> to permit children to engage in independent activities like walking to school or playing outside, becoming the first state to do so. Since then, <a href="https://letgrow.org/states/">12 states have amended neglect statutes</a> to recognize childhood independence, including Georgia. After media coverage of Patterson’s case, <a href="https://legiscan.com/GA/text/SB110/2025">Georgia lawmakers revised</a> the legal definition of neglect to allow children of sufficient maturity and ability to engage in independent activities, such as playing outdoors or running errands to a convenience store. The definition further added that neglect should involve blatant disregard of parental responsibilities resulting in a real, significant and imminent risk of harm to the child. </p>

<p>Yet despite these efforts, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/sop2.27">parents continue to be punished</a> for the decisions they’ve made when no harm was inflicted on the child.  </p>

<p>A finding of neglect carries serious consequences. It can impact a parent’s future employment and can result in a child’s removal from the home. Concurrent criminal charges can carry penalties of imprisonment, fines and other conditions like attending parenting classes and mandated compliance with child protective services directives. <a href="https://www.usnews.com/news/health-news/articles/2023-05-11/gender-reveals-data-shows-disparities-in-child-care-roles">Since mothers are more likely to be the primary caregiver</a>, they face increased exposure and scrutiny under these laws.</p>

<h2>Weighing safety against parental rights</h2>

<p>The Virginia General Assembly also <a href="https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/16.1-228/">amended its child neglect definition</a> in 2023 to clarify that children could engage in independent activities without adult supervision, like playing outdoors or traveling to nearby locations on foot or bicycle. It stipulated that  activities simply needed to be age-appropriate and the child would not be endangered, but it didn’t define a minimum age for when children could be unsupervised. </p>

<p>In other words, the Legislature left it to parents to determine when their child would be mature enough to participate in unsupervised activities. </p>

<p>So how did Karyann Parkinson, who had no history of abuse or neglect, still get caught up in the system?</p>

<p>In the police report, the officer noted that the 5-year-old was walking unattended about a half-mile from his home, in close proximity to a pond. The officer also added that Parkinson “demonstrated no remorse” and that she believed her son was mature enough to walk there and back for the feathers.</p>

<p>Parkinson has argued that she decided to allow her son to collect feathers on his own to instill confidence in him, not to put him at risk. Her son had been placed in <a href="https://thedailyrecord.com/2026/09/09/mother-charged-virginia-5-year-old-walks-pond-alone/">swimming lessons</a> to ensure he would be safe around bodies of water. </p>

<p>Police officers, social workers and prosecutors all share a fear of overlooking abuse or harm. And to be sure, this has also happened: In 2025, a 32-year-old Connecticut man set fire to a home where <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/04/08/nyregion/ct-waterbury-captive.html">he was allegedly being held captive for over two decades</a>. Ensuing reporting found that child protection authorities had failed to identify and stop the alleged abuse in the years prior, despite repeated concerns raised by teachers and schoolmates.</p>

<p>When serious cases like this one come to light, <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2015/10/28/us/bella-bond-massachusetts-child-abuse-case">the resulting media scrutiny</a> can expose agencies to public criticism <a href="https://www.wbur.org/news/2014/04/29/dcf-announcement-tuesday-morning">and cost state workers their jobs</a>. This scrutiny can create incentives for law enforcement and child welfare agencies to investigate cases thoroughly.</p>

<p>At the same time, it can also foster a culture of overreaction. </p>

<p>A commonsense approach to child protection balances safety with knowledge of the specific child and parents involved. And I don’t think it’s in a state’s interest to have frivolous cases consume limited resources, particularly given <a href="https://www.cwla.org/perspective-the-workforce-crisis-in-child-welfare-might-be-the-tip-of-an-iceberg/">the high turnover</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chiabu.2025.107319">heavy workloads</a> in child protective services.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293189/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>The science and politics behind the panic over ultraprocessed foods</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766598/original/file-20261015-50-qn8cgl.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=608%2C0%2C7115%2C4743&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Ultraprocessed foods make up a huge part of the global diet. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/unhealthy-products-food-bad-for-figure-skin-heart-royalty-free-image/1616586777"> beats3/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Ultraprocessed foods have a terrible reputation. </p>

<p>Studies have linked them with <a href="https://doi.org/10.1136/fmch-2026-003925">multiple chronic diseases</a>. Journalists and health influencers <a href="https://www.the-independent.com/health-and-fitness/ultraprocessed-food-health-risks-upf-b3007548.html">characterize them as poison</a>. Some public health experts call for <a href="https://www.thelancet.com/series-do/ultra-processed-food">a global halt</a> to producing and consuming them.</p>

<p>But the debate around ultraprocessed foods is not nearly as settled as it may seem. As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=4z-eSu4AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">researcher who studies social movements</a> for healthy and sustainable food, I have been documenting <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/acrefore/9780197762530.013.96">the history of processed foods</a> and examining <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/9780197859100.003.0068">debates around the science and politics of ultraprocessing</a>.</p>

<p>In basic terms, ultraprocessed foods are <a href="https://www.news-medical.net/health/How-Ultra-Processed-Foods-Are-Made-Inside-the-Industry-of-Engineered-Eating.aspx">mass-produced, industrial formulations</a> that use ingredients not typically found in a home kitchen, and that generally contain little to no intact whole foods. </p>

<p>Yet the very definition of ultraprocessed is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0007114522002793">highly contested</a>. While a growing number of advocates say that ultraprocessing is dangerous to public health, <a href="https://ggck2.substack.com/p/why-i-completely-disagree-with-ultra">skeptics counter</a> that the fervor around the topic has become a moral panic, and insist that some ultraprocessed foods can be part of a healthy diet. </p>

<h2>A brief history of food processing</h2>

<p>People have been <a href="https://www.ift.org/policy-and-advocacy/advocacy/toolkits/food-processing">processing food</a> – that is, transforming crops and animals into food ingredients and products – for all of human history. Cooking, which historians generally consider the <a href="https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/processed-food-a-two-million-year-history/">first form of food processing</a>, goes back as far as 2 million years. In the millennia and centuries that followed, people developed and refined other traditional food processing methods, including grinding, baking, fermenting, drying and pressing.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.3945/ajcn.114.089284">New types of food processing</a> were created during the industrial age, beginning in the mid-18th century. Canning, <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-pasteurization-a-dairy-expert-explains-how-it-protects-against-foodborne-illness-including-avian-flu-229335">pasteurization</a> and refrigeration were among the major innovations that reshaped not only how people eat but <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordhb/9780199729937.013.0015">society as a whole</a>.</p>

<p>Before that time, nearly all food was local food – that is, produced within a few dozen miles – and people consumed fresh foods quickly to avoid spoilage. Food processing promised to improve food safety, shelf life, quality, convenience, taste and healthfulness. The world became more urbanized as regional and international supply chains developed. Geographically dispersed farmers were connected to retailers and consumers across the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/03066150902820354">newly modern food system</a>.</p>

<p>From the mid-20th into the 21st century, food manufacturers added a host of complex technological innovations to the food processing playbook. Their efforts made processed foods more standardized for the mass market and more convenient for consumers. But public health experts warned that processed <a href="https://www.mcall.com/2017/12/28/how-to-fix-the-american-diet-according-to-the-man-who-coined-the-term-junk-food/">junk foods</a> were packed with <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/books/2013/feb/24/salt-sugar-fat-moss-review">salt, sugar and saturated fat</a> – <a href="https://abcnews.com/Health/government-dietary-guidelines-changed-years/story?id=36145436">problematic nutrients</a> linked to obesity, diabetes and other diet-related diseases. </p>

<h2>Food processing and the NOVA framework</h2>

<p>By the mid-2000s, some healthy food advocates began to argue that the nature and extent of food processing, rather than the presence of <a href="https://cup.columbia.edu/book/nutritionism/9780231156561/">specific problematic nutrients</a>, explained diet-related chronic disease. The journalist Michael Pollan famously implored his audience to avoid “<a href="https://michaelpollan.com/books/in-defense-of-food/">edible food-like substances</a>.” Instead, he advised: “Eat food. Not too much. Mostly plants.”</p>

<p>Brazilian epidemiologist Carlos Monteiro coined the term “ultraprocessing” in 2009 as part of his work on what he and colleagues called <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S1368980018003762">the NOVA classification</a>. The NOVA framework establishes a <a href="https://theconversation.com/maha-report-on-childrens-health-highlights-harms-of-ultraprocessed-foods-a-food-scientist-explains-the-research-257443">four-category system</a> that characterizes a food based on its level of processing. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766596/original/file-20261015-50-m558be.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A schematic of the four NOVA food processing categories - unprocessed foods, processed ingredients, processed foods and ultraprocessed foods" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766596/original/file-20261015-50-m558be.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766596/original/file-20261015-50-m558be.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=327&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766596/original/file-20261015-50-m558be.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=327&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766596/original/file-20261015-50-m558be.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=327&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766596/original/file-20261015-50-m558be.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=411&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766596/original/file-20261015-50-m558be.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=411&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766596/original/file-20261015-50-m558be.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=411&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">According to the NOVA classification developed by Brazilian epidemiologist Carlos Monteiro, ultraprocessed foods are defined as industrially manufactured food products that would be impossible to make at home.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/illustration/food-processing-classification-infographic-royalty-free-illustration/2273804269">Anastasia Usenko/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>NOVA Category 1 includes unprocessed or minimally processed plant or animal foods that are close to their natural state and contain no additives. Category 2 refers to processed culinary ingredients – that is, products derived from Category 1 via pressing, grinding or similar techniques. Category 3 describes processed foods made by combining Category 1 and Category 2 using traditional methods, such as baking, boiling or canning.</p>

<p>NOVA Category 4 foods are ultraprocessed foods, often described as industrially manufactured food products that can’t be made at home. Examples of ultraprocessing include separating whole foods into substances, chemically formulating foods or using cosmetic additives such as food dyes. </p>

<p>According to the framework, corporations design ultraprocessed foods to be <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S1368980017000234">convenient, hyperpalatable and highly profitable</a>. They are packaged attractively, marketed intensively and intended to displace other food groups.</p>

<p>Today, ultraprocessed foods make up an increasingly large <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajcnut.2026.101417">share of global diets</a>. They account for more than 50% of total calories <a href="https://www.npr.org/sections/shots-health-news/2025/08/07/nx-s1-5495308/ultra-processed-food-upf-rfk-cdc">in the United States</a>, with many <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ijpo.70002">low- and-middle income nations</a> not far behind. </p>

<h2>Unsettled science</h2>

<p>Since the NOVA framework emerged, researchers have tried to test whether food processing can explain how certain foods affect people’s health.</p>

<p>The vast majority of this work has explored correlations between consuming ultraprocessed foods and developing health problems. One consistent result stands out: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1136/fmch-2026-003925">People who consume more ultraprocessed foods</a> are at higher risk for multiple chronic diseases and early death.</p>

<p>However, even that conclusion is more complex than it appears. It turns out that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lana.2024.100859">certain categories of ultraprocessed foods</a> – such as sweetened beverages like sodas and processed meats like deli meats – are consistently associated with negative health outcomes including heart disease and stroke. But other ultraprocessed products – breads, cold cereals, yogurt and even savory snacks – have actually been correlated with lower rates of these health problems. </p>

<p>Still other ultraprocessed foods – including sauces, condiments and ready-to-heat dishes like frozen dinners – show no consistent links to people’s health one way or the other.</p>

<p>Only a handful of clinical trials that can actually show cause and effect have explored <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ensci.2025.100547">ultraprocessed foods’ effects on health</a>. One prominent study did find that participants who ate a diet of ultraprocessed foods for two weeks <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2019.05.008">consumed more calories and gained more weight</a> than participants who followed a minimally processed diet, but other experiments have <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aef3495">found no clear effect</a>. What’s more, these studies generally last just a few weeks – far too short a time frame to draw conclusions about long-term health impacts. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/aWGWCBY6lE4?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Many researchers point to studies linking ultraprocessed foods to chronic illnesses, though the ties are not as clear-cut as they might appear.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>A tricky definition</h2>

<p>Some food science researchers are unsurprised by these mixed findings, arguing that the definition of “ultraprocessed” is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41430-022-01099-1">ambiguous and frequently subjective</a>. For example, a cake prepared by a home baker would be considered a NOVA Category 3 “processed food.” But <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0954422422000117">if that same cake were industrially manufactured</a> using a commercial preservative, then packaged and sold at a grocery store, it would become a NOVA Category 4 “ultraprocessed food” – even if the two cakes were nutritionally identical. </p>

<p>Fundamentally, many nutrition scientists remain <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.advnut.2023.04.006">unconvinced that processing alone</a> can explain why certain foods are associated with poor health. Instead, they emphasize that unhealthy ultraprocessed foods frequently have poor nutritional profiles and other qualities that make them easy to overeat. And they argue that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2021.10.005%20External%20Link">making ultraprocessed foods healthier</a>, not getting rid of them entirely, can improve public health. </p>

<p>Vilifying ultraprocessed foods may have harms, they suggest, like <a href="https://theconversation.com/ultra-processed-food-why-the-debate-needs-less-fear-and-more-clarity-278060">creating unnecessary fear</a> and promoting <a href="https://www.skeptic.org.uk/2025/11/how-ultra-processed-food-fear-can-fuel-anxiety-and-disordered-eating/">disordered eating</a>. It can also stigmatize <a href="https://www.greenqueen.com.hk/ultra-processed-foods-list-plant-based-meat-guide/">eco-friendly, plant-based meats</a> or ultraprocessed products such as baby formula that are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/osp4.657">designed for clinical nutrition</a>. </p>

<p>The wholesale rejection of ultraprocessed foods could also make life more <a href="https://virginiasolesmith.substack.com/p/why-ultra-processed-foods-save-family-dinner">difficult for families</a> who rely on the convenience and affordability the products offer.</p>

<h2>Processing versus nutrients</h2>

<p>On the other hand, many food policy and public health researchers maintain that the common <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(25)01565-X">definition of ultraprocessed</a> is <a href="https://www.foodpolitics.com/2026/05/ultra-processed-food-defined-not-all-that-complicated/">clear enough</a>, especially if exceptions are made for healthy ultraprocessed foods. They also note that many supporters of ultraprocessed foods <a href="https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.2026.308591">have ties to the food industry</a>. They insist that the existing evidence is strong enough to <a href="https://healthyeatingresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/UPF-Expert-Panel-Executive-Summary-04.pdf">take immediate policy action</a>, including making changes to how ultraprocessed foods are produced, purchased and marketed. </p>

<p>Regulating ultraprocessed foods <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s43016-022-00599-4">wouldn’t just benefit public health</a>, advocates argue. It could also help rein in harms to <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2017/09/16/health/brazil-obesity-nestle.html">food culture, business and the environment</a>. </p>

<p>In this sense, ultraprocessed foods are a symptom of a bigger problem: an <a href="https://www.soilassociation.org/what-we-do/food/ultra-processed-foods/">unsustainable industrial food system</a> that is dominated by a handful of corporations. That argument, of course, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/08/opinion/food-industrial-local-organic.html">is plenty contested too</a>.   </p>

<p>Ultimately, researchers and advocates from all sides of the debate mostly agree that the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/10/opinion/food-environment-chronic-disease.html">modern food environment</a> needs to be made healthier. The key point of disagreement, however, is whether policymaking and dietary guidance should directly address ultraprocessing or stick to a more traditional focus on nutrients instead.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292661/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Why and how US and Canadian energy markets are so deeply intertwined</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765669/original/file-20261012-50-qhd5hd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=1512%2C1120%2C3844%2C2563&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The U.S. and Canadian economies are closely linked, especially around energy.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/and-canada-puzzle-pieces-partnership-and-royalty-free-image/2197015029">J Studios/DigitalVision via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/5979288-trump-imposes-canadian-tariffs/">50% tariffs imposed</a> by President Donald Trump’s administration on imports from Canada in July 2026, and the <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/carney-says-new-canadian-tariffs-us-goods-will-come-into-effect-september-8-2026-08-22/">reciprocal 50% tariffs imposed</a> by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s administration on imports to Canada from the U.S. a month later, do not include oil and natural gas. Electricity and some petroleum products were also left out, although they remain subject to a <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=67924">10% tariff</a> imposed in 2025. </p>

<p>That’s because the two countries’ energy systems and markets are so intertwined that tariffs would devastate both economies. Canada is the <a href="https://www.csis.org/analysis/mapping-us-canada-energy-relationship">biggest supplier of foreign petroleum</a> to the United States, supplying <a href="https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/oil-and-petroleum-products/imports-and-exports.php">half of all its petroleum imports</a>. It is also the only direct foreign supplier of electricity to the U.S., with <a href="https://www.csis.org/analysis/mapping-us-canada-energy-relationship">34 major transmission points</a> moving electricity from Canada south across the border.</p>

<p>In truth, Canada could <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/canada-should-be-ready-to-cut-electricity-critical-minerals-ontarios-premier-says">shut down those power links and leave thousands of Americans in the dark</a>, as Ontario provincial Premier Doug Ford threatened in August 2026. </p>

<p>But researchers like <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=DqcDs3YAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">me</a>, who study the historical links that have shaped Canadian and U.S. business relations, know that over the past 50 years Canada has expanded its energy production with one specific goal: serving U.S. consumption. In 2024, <a href="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/2fNWJ/1/">84% of Canadian oil production and 76% of Canadian electricity production</a> were exported to the U.S. Without American buyers, there is no real energy market in Canada.</p>

<p><iframe id="2fNWJ" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/2fNWJ/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A chart showing the high percentages of U.S. energy imports that come from Canada, and the high percentages of Canadian energy production that is exported to the U.S."></iframe></p>

<h2>Early connections</h2>

<p>Since the second half of the 19th century, energy generated on <a href="https://canadiangeographic.ca/articles/the-49th-parallel-our-defining-line/">both sides of the border</a> – and across them – has connected the two nations. The Great Lakes Basin was the hydraulic center of energy interconnectivity, as both nations shared the energy generated by Niagara Falls and the <a href="https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1939v02/ch13subch1">St. Lawrence River</a>.</p>

<p>During the early stages of World War II, even before the U.S. entered the fight, Canada and the U.S. started to integrate their energy systems. That work was part of <a href="https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1940v03/ch3subch1">joint security efforts to protect North America</a> through the integration of defense manufacturing production systems.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.treaty-accord.gc.ca/text-texte.aspx?id=100977">Ogdensburg Declaration</a> of 1940 and the 1941 <a href="https://www.treaty-accord.gc.ca/text-texte.aspx?id=103749">Hyde Park Declaration</a> consolidated and formalized the strategic economic and military cooperation between the two countries and set the foundations for future collaboration.  </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765672/original/file-20261012-50-jojfw4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A silhouette of a bridge with U.S. and Canadian flags flying on flagpoles." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765672/original/file-20261012-50-jojfw4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765672/original/file-20261012-50-jojfw4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765672/original/file-20261012-50-jojfw4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765672/original/file-20261012-50-jojfw4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765672/original/file-20261012-50-jojfw4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765672/original/file-20261012-50-jojfw4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765672/original/file-20261012-50-jojfw4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
