              <span class="caption">Ambassador Bridge, linking Windsor, Ontario, with Detroit, Mich., is just one of many border crossings vital to both nations’ economies.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/ambassador-bridge-winter-dusk-royalty-free-image/2260980123">Steven_Kriemadis/iStock / Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>From cooperation to integration</h2>

<p>After the war, Canadian and U.S. businesses liked the idea of sharing production and manufacturing operations, even beyond war-related work.</p>

<p>Nevertheless, manufacturing on both sides of the border went back to prewar ways of producing things domestically. Nationalist voices opposed the idea of further integrating the Canadian and U.S. economies.</p>

<p>Less than two decades after the war ended, though, the two nations signed the <a href="https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/canada-us-automotive-products-agreement">Auto Pact of 1965</a>, which eliminated tariffs on cars, trucks and automotive parts. Canadian parts manufacturers could compete directly with those based in the U.S., all to serve U.S. automakers.</p>

<p>This initial experiment in free trade revealed to businesses on both sides of the border that supply chain integration could benefit other production and service industries. </p>

<p>By 1989, the two countries had <a href="https://guides.ll.georgetown.edu/c.php?g=363556&amp;p=3662927">signed a full-scale free trade agreement</a> that removed tariffs for goods crossing the border in either direction. That opened the door for more closely integrating their energy markets too.</p>

<p>In 1992, a U.S. <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/102nd-congress/house-bill/776">federal law changed a wide swath of regulations</a> over the country’s energy markets. Some of the provisions allowed Canadian companies to sell excess energy to the U.S., and two years later the <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R42965">North American Free Trade Agreement</a> brought Mexico into the relationship too.</p>

<p>NAFTA integrated the production, processing and distribution of thousands of goods and services across all three countries.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765673/original/file-20261012-50-lvsdkg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A large concrete structure holds back a large body of water." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765673/original/file-20261012-50-lvsdkg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765673/original/file-20261012-50-lvsdkg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765673/original/file-20261012-50-lvsdkg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765673/original/file-20261012-50-lvsdkg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765673/original/file-20261012-50-lvsdkg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765673/original/file-20261012-50-lvsdkg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765673/original/file-20261012-50-lvsdkg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Hydro-Québec operates several dams on Canadian waterways that provide power not only to Canada but also to the U.S.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/view-of-hydro-quebecs-romaine-3-hydroelectric-dam-in-the-news-photo/1063934162">Lars Hagberg/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>But it was the interconnection of energy infrastructure that turned the Canadian and U.S. economies into one single energy market. Today, four major U.S. electrical grids depend on imported power from Canada: those serving the six <a href="https://www.iso-ne.com/about/key-stats/resource-mix">New England states</a>, <a href="https://www.nyiso.com/-/how-electricity-imports-from-canada-neighboring-states-support-grid-reliability">New York state</a>, <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=63684">15 states across the Midwest and the South</a>, and <a href="https://www.caiso.com/">California</a>. </p>

<p>Moreover, there are <a href="https://www.csis.org/analysis/mapping-us-canada-energy-relationship">more than 40 natural gas and petroleum liquids pipelines</a> connecting Canada with the United States. And although energy products move back and forth across the border, the <a href="https://www.csis.org/analysis/mapping-us-canada-energy-relationship">U.S. has an energy trade deficit</a> with Canada. Much of the U.S. economy runs on Canadian energy, and much of Canada’s energy production is sold to the U.S.</p>

<p>The current reality on the ground shows an integrated energy system between the two nations: something very difficult and costly to untangle, and a process that would take decades to reengineer. </p>

<p><iframe id="0Iwdn" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/0Iwdn/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A map showing the routes of oil and gas pipelines in Canada and the U.S."></iframe></p>

<h2>Local impact</h2>

<p>Today, those links form the basis for very tight integration between the two countries’ business and industrial marketplaces. </p>

<p>For example, Maine, where I live and work, gets close to <a href="https://wgme.com/news/i-team/how-reliant-is-maine-on-canadas-electrical-grid-new-brunswick-trade-war-trump-tariffs-central-maine-power-versant-maine-public-utilities-commission-power">30%  of its electricity</a> from Canada. </p>

<p>The state’s northern electrical grid is run by the <a href="https://tso.nbpower.com/public/en/op/">New Brunswick Power Corp.</a>, owned by the province of New Brunswick, which serves <a href="https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/new-brunswick/holt-electricity-trade-maine-1.7479544">close to 60,000</a> Mainers.</p>

<p>Today, Maine’s electric grid is owned mostly by foreign interests, including <a href="https://www.enmax.com/about-us/our-companies">ENMAX, the municipally owned utilities corporation of Calgary, Alberta</a>, and the owner of Versant Power, which serves 16% of Maine’s market. <a href="https://www.maine.gov/mpuc/regulated-utilities/electricity/delivery-rates">And 80%</a> is served by Central Maine Power, which is <a href="https://www.avangrid.com/">owned by Iberdrola</a> from Spain.</p>

<p>Canadian energy reaches deeper into the U.S., too. In 2025, Hydro-Quebec, a company that <a href="https://www.cmpco.com/w/another-major-milestone-toward-historic-agreement-to-bring-clean-energy-to-massachusetts">generates electricity from dams across the province of Quebec</a>, secured a deal with local regulators to use Maine as a corridor to supply clean energy to Massachusetts. Hydro-Quebec is <a href="https://www.hydroquebec.com/about/">owned by the government</a> of the province of Quebec. </p>

<p>The bilateral integration of energy infrastructure over the past 30-plus years explains why this sector was exempt from the most recent tariffs.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292090/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Electricity and some petroleum products were also left out, although they remain subject to a 10% tariff imposed in 2025

Canada is the biggest supplier of foreign petroleum to the United States, supplying half of all its petroleum imports
It is also the only direct foreign supplier of electricity to the U.S., with 34 major transmission points moving electricity from Canada south across the border

<title>How candidates are (quietly) talking about climate change – 3 election strategies you’ll see across the US</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764996/original/file-20261008-60-gxxv7x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7153%2C4768&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Supporters hold signs reading &#39;Make life affordable&#39; at a James Talarico Senate campaign stop in Houston.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/democratic-candidate-for-us-senate-james-talarico-speaks-news-photo/2294707557?phrase=James%20Talarico&amp;adppopup=true">Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Amid wars, inflation, emerging risks from artificial intelligence and threats to democracy, Americans have a lot to be worried about these days. But polls show the majority of <a href="https://climatecommunication.yale.edu/visualizations-data/ycom-us/">voters in 2026 are also concerned</a> about climate change as temperatures and disaster risks rise.</p>

<p>So why are <a href="https://insideclimatenews.org/news/24062026/analysis-shows-democrats-embrace-climate-hushing/">fewer candidates talking openly</a> about climate change in their midterm election campaigns than <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-83872-0_10">just a few years ago</a>? </p>

<p>At the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability, <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=b0-v3vAAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">we</a> <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=V_l0Y6MAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">study</a> <a href="https://looktomichigan.umich.edu/sif-projects/center-for-community-environmental-dialogue/">climate communication</a> and are following how Democratic candidates are discussing climate change in their campaigns.</p>

<p>Democratic candidates seem to agree on one strategy: campaign centrally on affordability, emphasizing how ordinary people are struggling to afford to <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/business/economy/consumer-sentiment-low-inflation-gas-rcna599890">fill up their cars</a>, <a href="https://powerlines.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/0511_PowerLines_Rising-Utility-Bills-Q1-2026.pdf">pay their electric bills</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s44168-025-00231-8">insure their homes</a> against hurricanes and wildfires. It’s part of a concerted effort to make the election a referendum on Republicans’ support for the Trump administration’s contributions to inflation, such as tariffs and the Iran war.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="An arial view of a neighborhood inundated with floodwater and the river behind where the levee breached." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/710343/original/file-20251225-56-nra1j0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C30%2C5085%2C3351&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/710343/original/file-20251225-56-nra1j0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/710343/original/file-20251225-56-nra1j0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/710343/original/file-20251225-56-nra1j0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/710343/original/file-20251225-56-nra1j0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/710343/original/file-20251225-56-nra1j0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/710343/original/file-20251225-56-nra1j0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Days of heavy rain broke levees in the Seattle area, engulfing this neighborhood in floodwater on Dec. 16, 2025. More Americans are experiencing extreme weather firsthand and connecting it to climate change.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/in-an-aerial-view-a-neighborhood-is-engulfed-in-floodwater-news-photo/2252270889">Brandon Bell/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Fossil fuel industry interests have <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-the-oil-industry-and-growing-political-divides-turned-climate-change-into-a-partisan-issue-243879">long sought to polarize</a> the public over the phrase “climate change.” As one of us, Geoffrey Henderson, discusses in <a href="https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262055642/getting-to-work-on-climate-policy/">his new book</a>, “Getting to Work on Climate Policy: The Strategy of Labor-Environmental Coalitions,” campaigns pitting economic concerns against environmental ones have made it harder to build support for policies meant to slow climate change.</p>

<p>When it comes to talking about climate change today, three distinct camps of Democratic candidates and officeholders reveal three different strategies.</p>

<h2>The energy populists</h2>

<p>The energy populists talk a lot about lowering energy prices for consumers but very little about either climate change or fossil fuels. </p>

<p>Many have been painting <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/25/sherrod-brown-data-center-unions-ohio-01092986">data centers</a>, rather than fossil fuel producers, as villains. Candidates often use messages focused on how utilities and data centers are raising voters’ electric rates. They propose measures to lower these costs, like requiring data centers to <a href="https://roycooper.com/costless/energy/">bring their own energy</a> sources onto the grid.</p>

<p>In North Carolina, former governor Roy Cooper, now running for U.S. Senate, emphasizes <a href="https://roycooper.com/costless/energy/">lowering energy and utility costs</a>. Sherrod Brown of Ohio, campaigning to return to the Senate, argues that his opponent’s votes in favor of data centers have led to “<a href="https://abc6onyourside.com/news/local/brown-targets-data-center-tax-breaks-and-rising-electric-bills-in-ohio-husted-politics-election-midterm-senate">higher electric rates</a>.”</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764027/original/file-20261005-50-m7yfar.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Roy Cooper meets with residents and his staff." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764027/original/file-20261005-50-m7yfar.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764027/original/file-20261005-50-m7yfar.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764027/original/file-20261005-50-m7yfar.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764027/original/file-20261005-50-m7yfar.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764027/original/file-20261005-50-m7yfar.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764027/original/file-20261005-50-m7yfar.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764027/original/file-20261005-50-m7yfar.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Roy Cooper, center, saw firsthand how disasters can ravage a state, including Hurricane Helene’s flooding that tore through mountain communities of North Carolina in 2024, killing more than 100 people.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.ncdps.gov/news/press-releases/2024/09/30/photovideo-available-governor-cooper-travels-western-nc-survey-storm-damage-hurricane-helene">North Carolina Department of Public Service</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Discussing energy affordability, without directly calling out the risks to the climate from burning fossil fuels or advocating for more renewable energy, aligns with the argument that <a href="https://www.searchlightinstitute.org/research/the-first-rule-about-solving-climate-change/">climate change messages can alienate swing voters</a>, who prioritize affordability.</p>

<p>If energy populists are elected, they could become silent backers of climate policies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions – both <a href="https://www.banking.senate.gov/newsroom/majority/brown-climate-change">Brown</a> and <a href="https://it.nc.gov/about/climate-change-clean-energy">Cooper</a> have a record of supporting renewable energy – or obstacles to climate policies.</p>

<h2>The climate champions</h2>

<p>Not all Democrats, even in battleground states, think climate change should fade into the background this election. However, few are as outspoken today as they were in the past.</p>

<p>In Massachusetts, Sen. Ed Markey’s website pledges that he will champion “<a href="https://www.edmarkey.com/issues-priorities/">bold action to invest in clean energy</a>” if reelected in November. In Maine, <a href="https://www.eenews.net/articles/lumberjack-lawmaker-troy-jackson-cuts-a-mixed-environmental-image/">Senate candidate Troy Jackson</a> asserts that politicians should not pit working-class people against renewable energy, casting the climate-versus-affordability debate as a false choice.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/sc7mMyujr1Q?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse from Rhode Island talks about candidates talking about climate change. Climate One.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Rhode Island’s Sheldon Whitehouse, one of the Senate’s most outspoken supporters of pro-climate policies, contends that <a href="https://energyempirepodcast.substack.com/p/senator-whitehouse-on-why-democrats">candidates should link higher costs to climate change</a>, such as increased home insurance costs due to hurricane risk. He also points to President Donald Trump’s blockade of the cheapest energy sources – <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/form-of-energy-cheapest-lazard-lcoe/">namely, solar and wind power</a> – which he attributes to fossil fuel industry influence.</p>

<p>If elected, these candidates’ messages suggest they will pursue policies that help reduce U.S. contributions to climate change. However, they may need to convince independent voters that their focus on climate change will not overshadow their attention to other challenges.</p>

<h2>The all-of-the-above proponents</h2>

<p>Another group of candidates wants to have it both ways. They call for actions that can respond to climate change and rapidly build out renewable energy, while also promising cheaper gasoline and more fossil fuel jobs. Scientists warn that more fossil fuel use <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03821-8">cuts against global climate goals</a>.</p>

<p>Unlike the other camps, this group does not identify villains in their narrative. These candidates are following the script from the Obama administration, whose <a href="https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/blog/2014/05/29/new-report-all-above-energy-strategy-path-sustainable-economic-growth">“all of the above” energy strategy</a> espoused continued fossil fuel use alongside policies to reduce planet-warming emissions.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/NzSmzd-5XY0?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Josh Turek, running for U.S. Senate from Iowa, talks with voters about high fuel costs. WHO13.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In Iowa, U.S. Senate candidate Josh Turek hosted a roundtable in April 2026 on how climate-fueled <a href="https://www.desmoinesregister.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/04/10/josh-turek-sheldon-whitehouse-insurance-rates-us-senate-race-iowa/89540786007/">extreme weather is raising insurance costs</a>. But he has also focused on <a href="https://iowacapitaldispatch.com/2026/09/21/turek-says-hes-happy-iowa-republicans-joined-his-push-for-diesel-export-pause/">lowering the cost of gasoline and diesel</a>. James Talarico, campaigning for the Senate in Texas, has similarly promised to fight climate change by <a href="https://jamestalarico.com/issue/energy-environment/">boosting renewable energy</a> while lowering costs by promoting all energy sources.</p>

<p>These candidates may be trying to signal their potential to support climate policies while respecting their states’ cultural connections to fossil fuels. Turek and Talarico are both running in <a href="https://www.nacleanenergy.com/wind/july-2025-wind-generation-by-state">states with abundant wind power</a>.</p>

<h2>Where are the voters on this issue?</h2>

<p>Studies from <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0007123417000321">the U.S.</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-026-03721-7">Germany</a> find that politicians usually underestimate public support for efforts to address climate change.</p>

<p>So how well do candidates’ platforms represent today’s voters?</p>

<p>Yale’s spring 2026 survey found that 49% of voters <a href="https://climatecommunication.yale.edu/publications/climate-change-in-the-american-mind-politics-policy-spring-2026/">believe global warming should be a high priority</a> for Congress and the president. But 70% of moderate or conservative Democrats share this view, alongside 84% of liberal Democrats. Even 1 in 3 liberal-to-moderate Republicans considers the climate a high priority.</p>

<p><iframe id="YBBTB" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/YBBTB/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Chart of voters' views on climate change as a priority for Congress and the president over time."></iframe></p>

<p>Yet polling also suggests that other issues, such as the increasing cost of living, are <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2026/07/23/as-the-2026-midterms-approach-economy-is-front-and-center/">even more important to many voters</a>. This data suggests that pro-climate messages could appeal to swing voters most strongly if climate policies are seen as complementary to affordability.</p>

<p>Still, a recent survey shows that voters open to Democratic candidates are <a href="https://www.2035initiative.com/climate-hush/">more likely to support</a> a candidate who prioritizes climate change. Climate messaging may especially resonate with young voters. Over a third of those ages 18 to 29 in a recent Harvard Youth Poll considered climate change an <a href="https://iop.harvard.edu/youth-poll/latest-poll">urgent national crisis</a>. Young Republicans are <a href="https://climatecommunication.yale.edu/publications/explore-16-years-of-u-s-climate-opinions-with-the-ccam-explore/">more supportive</a> of addressing climate change than their older counterparts.</p>

<p>While many shifts in the way candidates talk about climate policy have <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvp.2024.102482">little impact</a> on people’s willingness to participate in collective efforts to address it, messages emphasizing cost savings <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-022-01099-2">durably increase support</a> for renewable energy across party lines. Voters’ current concerns about inflation could make climate messages involving affordability especially effective in 2026, though the impact of these messages may <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-018-0122-0">vary from state to state</a>.</p>



<h2>Retail politics and the way forward</h2>

<p>These different approaches reflect the Democratic Party’s efforts to build a “big tent” that can attract voters with a wide range of views and priorities. Yet Democrats are generally coalescing around a message designed to appeal to working-class voters: that Trump and the Republicans are raising your cost of living. </p>

<p>November’s midterm elections will offer some insight into whether Democrats’ energy affordability message will resonate in the 2028 presidential election.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293687/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images Amid wars, inflation, emerging risks from artificial intelligence and threats to democracy, Americans have a lot to be worried about these days
But polls show the majority of voters in 2026 are also concerned about climate change as temperatures and disaster risks rise

So why are fewer candidates talking openly about climate change in their midterm election campaigns than just a few years ago ? At the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability, we study climate communication and are following how Democratic candidates are discussing climate change in their campaigns

Democratic candidates seem to agree on one strategy: campaign centrally on affordability, emphasizing how ordinary people are struggling to afford to fill up their cars , pay their electric bills and insure their homes against hurricanes and wildfires
It’s part of a concerted effort to make the election a referendum on Republicans’ support for the Trump administration’s contributions to inflation, such as tariffs and the Iran war
Days of heavy rain broke levees in the Seattle area, engulfing this neighborhood in floodwater on Dec. 16, 2025
More Americans are experiencing extreme weather firsthand and connecting it to climate change

Brandon Bell/Getty Images Fossil fuel industry interests have long sought to polarize the public over the phrase “climate change.” As one of us, Geoffrey Henderson, discusses in his new book , “Getting to Work on Climate Policy: The Strategy of Labor-Environmental Coalitions,” campaigns pitting economic concerns against environmental ones have made it harder to build support for policies meant to slow climate change
When it comes to talking about climate change today, three distinct camps of Democratic candidates and officeholders reveal three different strategies
The energy populists The energy populists talk a lot about lowering energy prices for consumers but very little about either climate change or fossil fuels
Many have been painting data centers , rather than fossil fuel producers, as villains
Candidates often use messages focused on how utilities and data centers are raising voters’ electric rates
They propose measures to lower these costs, like requiring data centers to bring their own energy sources onto the grid
In North Carolina, former governor Roy Cooper, now running for U.S
Senate, emphasizes lowering energy and utility costs

Sherrod Brown of Ohio, campaigning to return to the Senate, argues that his opponent’s votes in favor of data centers have led to “ higher electric rates .” Roy Cooper, center, saw firsthand how disasters can ravage a state, including Hurricane Helene’s flooding that tore through mountain communities of North Carolina in 2024, killing more than 100 people

North Carolina Department of Public Service Discussing energy affordability, without directly calling out the risks to the climate from burning fossil fuels or advocating for more renewable energy, aligns with the argument that climate change messages can alienate swing voters , who prioritize affordability

If energy populists are elected, they could become silent backers of climate policies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions – both Brown and Cooper have a record of supporting renewable energy – or obstacles to climate policies
The climate champions Not all Democrats, even in battleground states, think climate change should fade into the background this election
However, few are as outspoken today as they were in the past
Ed Markey’s website pledges that he will champion “ bold action to invest in clean energy ” if reelected in November
In Maine, Senate candidate Troy Jackson asserts that politicians should not pit working-class people against renewable energy, casting the climate-versus-affordability debate as a false choice
Sheldon Whitehouse from Rhode Island talks about candidates talking about climate change

Rhode Island’s Sheldon Whitehouse, one of the Senate’s most outspoken supporters of pro-climate policies, contends that candidates should link higher costs to climate change , such as increased home insurance costs due to hurricane risk
He also points to President Donald Trump’s blockade of the cheapest energy sources – namely, solar and wind power – which he attributes to fossil fuel industry influence
If elected, these candidates’ messages suggest they will pursue policies that help reduce U.S. contributions to climate change
However, they may need to convince independent voters that their focus on climate change will not overshadow their attention to other challenges
The all-of-the-above proponents Another group of candidates wants to have it both ways
They call for actions that can respond to climate change and rapidly build out renewable energy, while also promising cheaper gasoline and more fossil fuel jobs
Scientists warn that more fossil fuel use cuts against global climate goals
Unlike the other camps, this group does not identify villains in their narrative

These candidates are following the script from the Obama administration, whose “all of the above” energy strategy espoused continued fossil fuel use alongside policies to reduce planet-warming emissions
Senate from Iowa, talks with voters about high fuel costs
Senate candidate Josh Turek hosted a roundtable in April 2026 on how climate-fueled extreme weather is raising insurance costs
But he has also focused on lowering the cost of gasoline and diesel
James Talarico, campaigning for the Senate in Texas, has similarly promised to fight climate change by boosting renewable energy while lowering costs by promoting all energy sources
These candidates may be trying to signal their potential to support climate policies while respecting their states’ cultural connections to fossil fuels
Turek and Talarico are both running in states with abundant wind power
Where are the voters on this issue? Studies from the U.S. and Germany find that politicians usually underestimate public support for efforts to address climate change

title: Why the Trump administration is fighting over a golf course
excerpt: A golfer plays on the course at East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, DC, on October 19, 2026. | Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in  Th
body: A golfer plays on the course at East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, DC, on October 19, 2026. | Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump is trying to take over a public park.  What’s happening? On Sunday, Trump announced in a social media post that East Potomac Golf Links, a municipal golf course on the Potomac River in Washington, DC, would close next month for what he described as “restoration work” to transform it from a three-course complex into a single professional-caliber course.  According to a rendering of the “restoration” shared by Trump, the new course would also eliminate a popular public park and multiuse road around the course, which is currently home to some of DC’s historic cherry trees.  Why does this matter? Relative to many other Trump decisions (like, say, the Iran war or interfering with Ukraine’s ability to defend itself), the fate of a golf course is not so high-stakes

But it’s shaping up to be a major legal fight over the administration’s blitzkrieg approach to Washington that saw the East Wing of the White House demolished last year and Trump’s name attached to (and subsequently removed from) the Kennedy Center
A DC preservation group previously sued over Trump’s plan to transform the course, which has been in the works for months prior to Sunday’s announcement

And the administration was already in hot water with a DC District Court judge over the recent removal of more than 500 trees from the course, which it described at the time as maintenance rather than part of Trump’s renovation scheme.  Trump, for his part, has said that his administration has “an absolute right” to renovate the course and does not need approval, setting him on a course for a bigger clash with federal courts.  What’s the big picture? Setting aside everything else about Trump’s golf course push, it’s unlikely — with just 15 days until the midterms — that this is a fight that will endear him or his party to voters, who are broadly fed up with corruption, inflation, and the overall cost of living

And with that, it’s time to log off… Hi readers, happy Monday! Early voting is getting underway in some states and while The Logoff officially encourages you not to read too much — or anything, really — into early voting numbers, I do recommend this post from the Substack newsletter Can We Still Govern? by Don Moynihan
He rounded up some of the best “I voted” stickers with art submitted by (mostly) children, ranging from charming to deeply strange
As always, thanks for reading, have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!

title: The French youth revolt
excerpt: A protester holds a smoke flare and French flag during a demonstration at Paris’s Place de la Republique on October 17, 2026. | Kiran Ridley/AFP via Getty Image
body: A protester holds a smoke flare and French flag during a demonstration at Paris’s Place de la Republique on October 17, 2026. | Kiran Ridley/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day
French protests have long been the stuff of legend, literature, and Broadway musicals
But even by those storied standards, last weekend’s demonstrations were pretty remarkable
More than half a million people took to the streets in occasionally violent protests that are posing a mounting political challenge for the French government

The movement began roughly a month ago over concerns about the sorry state of public high schools , which are frequently underfunded and understaffed.  But in the weeks since, the student protests have rapidly expanded to encompass a wider range of grievances around inequality, high living costs and public services

The ranks of the protesters have also swelled to include some more opportunistic looters and agitators .   In Paris, masked rioters trashed businesses and set fires, while students blocked the Louvre Museum on Monday, forcing it to close
In Limoges, a city of roughly 130,000 people, the spire of a 19th-century town hall dramatically collapsed in flames
The national government has responded with curfews for parts of cities including Paris, Nice, and Lille, as well as emphatic condemnations of the violence

In a televised address on Sunday night, French President Emmanuel Macron also promised to partner with students, teachers, trade unions and other groups to identify “joint solutions.” But it’s unclear what solutions could possibly speak to the whole of this newly expanded movement
The initial student protesters were after concrete educational reforms, like smaller class sizes and less chaotic schedules
The demands now are more diffuse and disjointed, reflecting the sense that — as Macron himself put it — “there is no desirable future” for young people in France
It’s a situation that the French far right is already exploiting , just six months before the country’s next presidential election
Go a little deeper View Link If you’re getting a bit of déjà vu here — that’s French for “already seen,” FYI — please know you have good reason
The French also turned out for gigantic mass protests against a proposed retirement age increase three years ago
And a gas-tax hike five years before that
Some historians trace French protest culture all the way back to the 1300s
While it’s not necessarily true that the French demonstrate more than people in other Western countries, their protests do tend to attract outsize global attention
Youth protests over education, living costs, and government corruption have also recently taken place in Belgium, Portugal, Italy, Spain, and Albania, for instance
I’d hazard that you’ve heard less about them
But there’s a twofold explanation for why France’s protests loom so large
First, protest occupies a special place in French history and culture — and the world knows it

As one political scientist explained in a 1994 paper on the history of French protests, the French have an unusual, centuries-long track record of turning demonstrations into actual political change, arguably starting with the French Revolution
More recently, in 1968, student protests expanded into a larger worker strike that nearly toppled the government
Many of today’s young protesters have specifically referenced that heritage in interviews and slogans
But that’s not the only reason that French people always seem to be protesting
Conditions in France are also, well … pretty protestable
Consider just the narrow issue of public education, which sparked the current hullabaloo.  By some estimates, higher-education funding per student has fallen by 20 percent in just the past 10 years

High school classrooms are frequently overcrowded , and a government report cited by The Guardian concluded that the country’s aging schools are in need of billions of dollars of building repairs and climate mitigation

The government has pointed to France’s strained finances as a constraint on addressing these issues. (And, in fairness, France’s finances are indeed very strained .) There’s a sense, however, that young people are bearing the cost of that crisis more than other populations
Cost-cutting measures that would affect older people — such as raising the retirement age from 62 to 64 — have been delayed in the face of fierce opposition
And by “opposition,” of course, I mean protests.  One link for later ➨ Make your AI fallback plan
Artificial intelligence will cost many people their jobs; in some places, it already has
But instead of panic-learning the first available trade, first consider where you find meaning in your current occupation
That should help guide you to a fallback career that will still feel valuable, even if it’s…you know

My colleague Sigal says she’d become a rabbi; I think I’d like to teach again.  Before you go… Did you know… that a single episode of Sex and the City is credited with launching the early aughts cupcake craze? Today’s food trends are much shorter-lived, by comparison

And they typically start on TikTok or Instagram.  Today’s trivia: What mass-market, imported beer is named for a river in the Netherlands? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Last week we asked you for the author of the 1952 self-help book The Power of Positive Thinking
That would be Norman Vincent Peale, the Protestant minister who also preached at President Donald Trump’s childhood church and officiated his first wedding.

title: How the Iran war is ruining Saudi Arabia’s plans
excerpt: Flames burn at a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco south of Riyadh on October 3, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images As the US-Iran war drags on, the damage
body: Flames burn at a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco south of Riyadh on October 3, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images As the US-Iran war drags on, the damage is being felt regionally: Saudi Arabia experienced the worst attack in over a decade earlier this month, when Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi militia struck an airport in the Saudi capital , Riyadh
The strike killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 others

Saudi Arabia responded with missile attacks on Yemen, striking oil facilities , and the Houthis have launched more strikes of their own, targeting Saudi oil infrastructure .  The dueling strikes are the latest development in a decade-plus of conflict between Saudi and the Houthis, a political and military group that controls part of northern Yemen, which had been on pause until earlier this year after a 2022 ceasefire

But the Iran war, and Houthi affiliation with Iran’s network of proxy groups, mean the current violence has far-reaching implications for the US, Israel, and the global energy economy.  It also threatens more than just Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil industry: As Gregg Carlstrom , a Middle East correspondent for The Economist, explains, the attacks cut at the heart of the country’s project to evolve into a destination for foreign investment, travel, tourism, and more
On Monday, the country’s upcoming Future Investment Initiative was postponed until 2027

Carlstrom, who is based in Riyadh, spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram how the attack has been received inside Saudi Arabia, why it comes at an especially bad time for the country, and how President Donald Trump might — or might not — get more involved.  Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
Can you help us understand how the Houthis have such a presence in the country right now? Are they infiltrating the country? Are they already there? They’re shooting from outside the country
The Houthis are a group that’s been around for a few decades
They were originally a local insurgency in Yemen that was fighting against the Yemeni government
They originate from the northern part of Yemen, but they were able to gain control of large parts of that country from 2014 onwards

Ali Abdullah Saleh, the longtime dictator of Yemen, was overthrown during the Arab Spring and the Houthis were able to seize a large chunk of territory.  They are effectively in control of most of the population centers in Yemen
They have received increasing support from Iran, which has provided them with weapons, with money, with know-how, and technical expertise
And they have used that to build an arsenal of drones and missiles, which they are using now to carry out attacks on Saudi Arabia

And was there a particular reason they targeted the airport in Riyadh? Were they trying to send a message here? If you listen to the messaging from the Houthis, they are trying to describe this as almost a like-for-like campaign, where you’ve had years in which the Saudi-led coalition, which invaded Yemen in 2015, has been imposing a blockade of Yemeni airspace, has been restricting flights in and out of that country.  And so the Houthis describe this publicly as being a retaliation in kind, but I think they’ve also just figured out that attacks on airports are a very effective way to cause economic disruption in Saudi Arabia

You prevent not just people from flying in and out but also, as we’ve seen disruptions to shipping via the Strait of Hormuz, a lot of cargo that these countries depend on for daily needs are coming in by air instead.  Carrying out these sorts of attacks, shutting down the airport in a capital city, is a very effective way for the Houthis to impose economic pain on the Saudis
And I guess on some level it makes the country feel insecure

How is that making Saudi Arabia’s leader feel right now? What’s his response been? It comes at a very difficult time for the Saudi leadership because they are supposed to be hosting a number of events this month where Saudi will be playing a role on the world stage.  There’s something called the World Petroleum Congress that is taking place this week [October 11–15], which is normally a big event that draws executives from top oil and gas companies

Many of them canceled their participation because of the attacks on the airport.  Then they are supposed to be hosting the [now- postponed ] Future Investment Initiative, which is something often known outside Saudi Arabia as “Davos in the Desert.” It’s the sort of flagship investment conference that takes place here every year

It draws a who’s who of global finance.  For a country that is trying to diversify its economy, a country that is trying to attract foreign investment and make itself into a hub for finance and travel and tourism, these sorts of attacks are very detrimental to those goals
And this is coming as Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and the rest of the leadership in the country is really trying to establish Saudi Arabia as the premier economic hub in the region
The stakes are really high for him right now? They are

And just about everything that they are trying to do is being disrupted by what’s happened over the past few weeks.  If you look at travel, for example, the Public Investment Fund, which is the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, last year launched a new airline, Riyadh Air, which they are hoping will eventually compete with Emirates or Qatar Airways, the really big carriers in the Gulf.   That airline was just getting into regular operations this summer where they were growing their fleet, they were growing their network of destinations
And then suddenly this happens and their home base in Riyadh is shut down
They have moved some of their planes out of Riyadh to other airports to keep them safe from Houthi attacks

Obviously, it’s very disruptive for trying to build an air carrier.  In Riyadh itself, the financial district — this sort of long-planned attempt to set up a banking hub that might rival the one in Dubai — had just started to get going over the past couple of years, when you had banks and other financial services firms moving in there

Everybody who works there has now been told to work remotely for the foreseeable future because there is a concern about possible Houthi attacks against skyscrapers and the financial district.  Everything they are trying to do, from finance to travel to trade, all of it is being disrupted and threatened by what’s happening in Yemen

What options does he have to reassure investors and the world really that he can protect the country and maybe especially his airport, where a bunch of the investment is focused? The airport, I think, is going to be difficult to reassure people about
You can install additional air defenses there
You can move more batteries and more interceptors there, but at the end of the day, no air defense system is hermetic

There’s no 100 percent guarantee that you’re going to shoot down every incoming projectile.  As long as there is this ongoing war between the Houthis and Yemen and the Saudis, I think people might have ongoing concerns about the airport
You have to resolve that underlying issue to give people confidence.  Now, how do you try to resolve that? If you’re Saudi Arabia right now, you have two bad options
You try to militarily defeat the Houthis or at least force them to accept a renewed ceasefire.  The other option is you cut a deal
You try to offer the Houthis some concessions that might encourage them to go back to the ceasefire
That’s going to be very costly for Saudi Arabia

I’ve heard that the Houthis are demanding probably billions of dollars of financial concessions where they would want the Saudis to offer some money for reconstruction and to pay the salaries of Yemeni civil servants working in Houthi-controlled areas.  If you are the Saudi leadership right now, neither one is really a good option
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has a pretty strong relationship with the president of the United States, who’s very sympathetic to Saudi Arabia and Saudi investment
Has he appealed to President Trump for help here yet? He has
He’s done so repeatedly over the past month or so, asking not just for support with the Saudi campaign in Yemen, but for America to carry out its own airstrikes in Yemen
And the response so far from Donald Trump has been to refuse that

title: We all want to offload our most tedious tasks. But what do we lose in the process?
excerpt: If there’s one thing a busy person doesn’t need, it’s more information
body: If there’s one thing a busy person doesn’t need, it’s more information
More emails, more notifications, more infinite feeds — the steady drip of data spells doom for the overstimulated American
And if you’re a busy parent, like me, sometimes it feels like a flood: school emails, doctor’s appointments, so many little things to buy
Even things that used to be simple are harder

I recently listed an item on Facebook Marketplace, which quickly meant I was replying to offers and getting ghosted for the better part of a weekend before finding someone who, after a detailed back-and-forth about the most likely place to find a parking spot in my neighborhood, finally took my old baby swing away

You’ve probably seen the ads on Instagram promising “AI that gets it done for you.” The new personal AI agent app from Meta can not only automate your Facebook Marketplace tasks, but also sort your emails, manage your calendar, and buy your groceries
And it’s free — unless you’re using it most of the day or you want access to Meta’s most powerful models , at which point it costs $20 or $100 a month

Muse is probably the personal AI agent you’ve heard of — and it’s currently the market leader with more than 8 million downloads in its first month, according to one estimate — but there’s now a small army of these bots: OpenAI recently announced Dots , X has Grok Bot , and there’s Instinct , which is currently invite-only and operates entirely in iMessage or WhatsApp
They all offer the same promise: to remove friction from your busy life
For the last two weeks, I’ve been handing over more and more of my life to AI agents in pursuit of making my life a little simpler
What I found is that AI is unpredictable, and so are AI agents
When I first began using Muse, it started doing things I didn’t ask it to do
It offered to help with random email threads and created dossiers on people in my work meetings
It generated a detailed report on nearby apple-picking destinations based on a calendar invite from my wife
To me, an AI agent doing these things without prompting isn’t helpful

It’s unnerving.  But ultimately, I came away believing that AI agents can make your life easier.  That might mean giving an AI agent more access than you’re comfortable with — handing over lots of login credentials and possibly even your credit card
The more you rely on an AI agent, the more you risk outsourcing your decision-making

This raises real questions about how much agency we want to hold onto in our lives — even the tedious parts.  The leap of faith Let’s get one thing out of the way first: To make an agent work for you, you’ll have to sacrifice a tremendous amount of privacy and grant it permission to access a lot of personal information.  Muse and its competitors can do the classic generative AI tricks, like draft emails or make you a fitness plan
If you’d like the agent to send one of those emails, however, you’ll have to grant it permission to access pretty much everything in your Gmail account
If you want it to schedule workouts, it will need access to your calendar
If you want the agent to buy anything on your behalf, it will need your credit card
If you want it to book your doctor’s appointments, it will need the credentials to log into your healthcare portal

The more permission you grant it, the more the agent can do for you, but that also opens up more opportunities for the agent to misunderstand you or your instructions (more on this in a moment).  This process of sharing your digital life with an AI agent means you’re giving an untold amount of personal information to tech companies, who don’t always behave ethically , and who sell user data for profit

For now, Meta says that it does not share Muse data or conversations with its ad systems, although privacy experts warn that doesn’t really matter since those systems monitor what Muse does on your behalf
Nevertheless, Muse’s early days were filled with security and privacy blunders
But without all of this info and access, the AI agents aren’t very useful
So if you’re not comfortable letting a bot into all of your accounts, an AI agent is probably never going to be the solution to your digital administrative exhaustion

But even if you are willing to hand that over, there are still other barriers to an agent’s efficiency and effectiveness.  The blank slate problem AI agents, like a lot of new software tools (including chatbots), suffer from the blank slate problem
The blank slate problem essentially means that people don’t know how to get started
This might be because you don’t know about the tool’s capabilities, or because you simply don’t know what would be helpful
As with AI in general, we don’t exactly know how AI agents work

That means we don’t know exactly what they can do or how they’ll do it, according to Pattie Maes , a professor of media technology at MIT — so it’s necessary to do a lot of babysitting. “I feel like I’m not gaining a lot of time because I can’t completely trust the system,” Maes told me about her experience with Muse, “and I can’t predict how it will behave and what it will do.”  Some advice I heard from early adopters of these tools, however, is to start small. “In the beginning, it’s very hard to trust that it’s going to just magically do a really big thing,” Julie Zhuo , founder of the AI company Sundial and an early Facebook employee, told me about her experience using personal agents. “So you give it smaller tasks, and once you see it succeed, then I feel like you develop more trust that it can tackle bigger things.” This is surely why Meta decided that Muse needed an Ideas tab full of small tasks the AI agent can do
Muse will also send you a lot of push notifications to prompt you to do stuff, like reply to specific emails or prepare for a meeting
That detailed report on apple-picking destinations? That was a notification about something I didn’t ask Muse to do

Muse also sent me a notification about a show hosted by a podcast I don’t listen to and another one with details about a Halloween party I wasn’t invited to, as well as several evening digests that included lists of things it had already bugged me about that day
Notifications are either helpful nudges or time-consuming attention thieves, depending on your worldview
However, if you fall into the latter category and turn off the notifications from your always-on personal agent, you’re inevitably forfeiting some friction reduction opportunities

This gets to the heart of one of the big questions I have about AI agents: How helpful are they, really, if it’s this difficult to know what to do with them? These agents worked much better when I drove the conversation
While wondering what to do with my new agents, literally staring at the blank slate, cost me some time, I found myself thrilled at how easy basic productivity tasks became

Adding events to my calendar, making to-do lists and then being held accountable for stuff not getting done, being reminded to reply to an email — it was these kinds of simple, administrative chores where I saw personal AI agents really start to save me time.  Other tech journalists seemed to have similar experiences

title: The Republicans worried that AI will bring an “age of darkness”
excerpt: Ron DeSantis speaks during a press conference on June 6, 2023 in Wildwood, Florida. | Paul Hennessy/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images If President Donald Trump ha
body: Ron DeSantis speaks during a press conference on June 6, 2023 in Wildwood, Florida. | Paul Hennessy/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images If President Donald Trump had his way, the Republican Party would be top-to-bottom the party of AI — or, in his preferred branding, “super intelligence.” But down in the very state where Trump has his “ winter White House ,” two Republicans have put forth a very different vision for the party’s future — and have been far more eager to take on the artificial intelligence industry
Ron DeSantis and his attorney general, James Uthmeier, have become vocal critics of the AI industry over the past year, warning of the technology’s dangers to children and to humanity as a whole
This sets them apart from Trump, who has championed the industry and downplayed its dangers
DeSantis tried to pass an “AI bill of rights” with child safety restrictions, but his effort was foiled by other Florida Republicans with close White House ties
Uthmeier has filed a wide-ranging lawsuit against OpenAI and the company’s CEO, Sam Altman
The two are betting that public backlash against AI will grow deeper, including among Republicans — and they’re hoping they’ll be able to steer the party in a post-Trump world
Ron DeSantis, who devoted much of his final year in office to a failed effort to pass an “AI bill of rights,” which would have imposed tougher restrictions regarding child safety and other topics

He’s warned that AI could “set off an age of darkness and deceit,” blasted “tech oligarchs” for putting people at risk, and called Anthropic “very creepy” for exploring whether AI could be conscious. “He clearly understands what the risks are, and I find he’s also very good at calling bullshit on disingenuous arguments from the Silicon Valley lobby,” Max Tegmark, an MIT physicist who co-founded the Future of Life Institute, an AI safety nonprofit, told me. (DeSantis hosted Tegmark at two events in Florida this year.) The other is DeSantis’s handpicked attorney general, James Uthmeier, a longtime close ally who is now trying to win the AG’s office in his own right — and who filed a high-profile lawsuit against OpenAI in June

Last week, Uthmeier asked the judge in the case to block OpenAI from developing new models unless they had “independent third-party guardrails and approval.” “The danger of these AI systems is real and growing,” Forrest Saunders, a spokesperson for Uthmeier, told me. “Florida and the nation have seen case after case of violence, child exploitation, and models that operate beyond their developer’s control.” He added that Uthmeier “welcomes innovation, but Floridians will not be the test subjects.” With AI cresting as a national anxiety — or a national opportunity, depending who you talk to — both major parties are still finding their footing on the issue

And though Trump is clearly trying to get Republicans in lockstep behind the industry, a very strong current is pulling the other way, responding to populist concerns and parents’ complaints to stake out a much more skeptical position. Florida has emerged as a bellwether for what Republican policies might look like if conservative America turns decisively against AI, especially as Trump’s political clock runs out

DeSantis and Uthmeier aren’t unique in the GOP for having concerns about AI — a handful of House members and senators want further action , and populist opposition to data centers has bubbled up in races around the country

But the two have gone furthest in taking on the industry directly — and they’ve done so even though it puts them on the wrong side of Trump.  In recent days, I spoke to several Florida political observers and advocates on the AI issue

Most believe that DeSantis and Uthmeier are affirmatively trying to stake out what the GOP’s position on AI should be in a post-Trump future, and to better align with an electorate that’s turning sharply against the industry, despite what the president may say.  “He’s trying to skate where the puck is going,” Jeff Brandes, a former Republican state senator, told me. (DeSantis’s office did not respond to a request for comment.) Beyond the quest for political advantage, the stakes are very real

Will there actually be a significant and influential force on the right that takes the concerns about advanced AI’s harms seriously — and is willing to act to try and rein them in, before they do great damage?  DeSantis and Uthmeier are hoping the answer is yes — and that they will be the ones leading that charge
Ron DeSantis’s quest for an AI bill of rights In this case, the politics and the personal are intertwined

DeSantis occupies a unique place within the party at this particular moment that’s given him an incentive to buck the national consensus on the right, especially when it comes to Trump, and explore an independent approach
In his first decade in politics, DeSantis had a charmed rise
In 2012, he embraced the Tea Party to win a seat in Congress; in 2017, he bear-hugged Trump to get his endorsement for governor

He then became a national conservative star for opposing pandemic-era public health restrictions and waging war on “wokeness,” winning his 2022 reelection in a nearly 20-point landslide. “He is always out front, even ahead of other Republicans, on issues that he makes more important,” Peter Schorsch, editor of Florida Politics, told me. “I would joke with people that I didn’t know how to spell ESG or DEI before he brought these to the forefront.” But what followed was a failed presidential primary campaign that put DeSantis on the wrong side of Trump and then sent him back to Florida with an uncertain political future.  Early last year, just weeks after a report that DeSantis’s wife Casey was considering running to succeed him as governor, Trump publicly urged Rep

Byron Donalds to enter the race, promising his “Complete and Total Endorsement.” Also early last year, DeSantis, who had long run roughshod over Republican legislators, was faced with a new thorn in his side: an ambitious new state house speaker, Daniel Perez, who was more interested in cultivating the Trump White House than the governor

Perez took a far more assertive stance in shaping legislation and rejecting some of the governor’s demands than his predecessors; he also publicly blessed an investigation into a charity tied to Casey DeSantis
A bitterly personal feud between Perez and DeSantis ensued

In the midst of all this, last summer, DeSantis got AI-pilled.  In July 2025, DeSantis announced that he was going to develop a state plan to deal with the rise of artificial intelligence. “We can’t just turn the reins over to a bunch of tech overlords,” he said . (DeSantis had long been a critic of major tech and social media companies on the grounds that they are too “woke” or politically hostile to conservatives and their ideas.) At another event that month, DeSantis said : “I think this is, like, the biggest issue that’s facing our society.” He mentioned AI’s potential impacts on the economy , on jobs, on students, and on the spread of “false narratives” as troubling to him. “I welcome technologies that will enhance the human experience
I do not welcome things that are going to supplant the human experience,” DeSantis said in September

His interest in state action put him on the opposite side of the Trump administration, which was advocating for a 10-year moratorium on state regulation of AI — arguing that forcing the industry to abide by a patchwork of state regulations would slow its growth. ( David Sacks , a key Trump adviser on AI, championed this argument .) Last December, at the Florida mega-retirement community the Villages, DeSantis rolled out his proposed “ AI bill of rights .” It did not focus on existential or civilizational risks, but instead more practical concerns around child safety
Megan Garcia, a Florida mother whose 14-year-old son died by suicide after conversing with a chatbot “companion,” appeared at the press conference

As introduced in the Florida state senate, the bill would have required that parents consent to minors speaking to companion chatbots and forced companies to disclose when users weren’t speaking to a human, among other provisions

But it was dead on arrival in the Florida House of Representatives — where Perez had aligned himself closely with the White House. “We do believe that the federal government should take care of AI, and whatever legislation or policy has to pass on a national level,” Perez said .  Brendan Steinhauser, who heads the AI safety advocacy group Alliance for Secure AI, told me that he saw Perez at a Mar-a-Lago fundraiser around this time, and asked him about safety risks. “He leaned to me and whispered, ‘We’re with you, but the president has made it clear not to move forward on this stuff,’” Steinhauser said. “So, the White House basically put the kibosh on that effort.”  DeSantis complained publicly that Perez was pursuing a “personal agenda” and thwarting badly needed legislation
It was to no avail — the bill didn’t move

But Perez did — Trump nominated him as ambassador to Brazil in June, and he was confirmed in August . (A request for comment from Perez, submitted to the State Department, received no response.) James Uthmeier’s lawsuit against OpenAI Though DeSantis hit a wall in the legislature, his attorney general was soon waging his own battle against OpenAI in court
The attorney general is an elected position in Florida, but when Marco Rubio vacated his Senate seat to become secretary of state, DeSantis filled the seat with the state AG, Ashley Moody

Then, to fill the newly vacant AG job, DeSantis chose one of his closest aides, who had served as his general counsel, chief of staff, presidential campaign manager, and chief of staff again — Uthmeier.  Uthmeier is a Florida native who had worked in Rubio’s Senate office; he graduated from Georgetown Law School in 2014

After that he joined the firm Jones Day and worked with Don McGahn ; when McGahn was named White House counsel in Trump’s first term, Uthmeier went with him to the new administration, ending up at the Commerce Department
Then, in 2019, he headed back to his home state to work for the new governor, DeSantis, and has been close by his side ever since

Now, though, DeSantis is term-limited, and Uthmeier is trying to get Florida voters to elect him for a full term as AG on his own. ( Trump’s allies had reportedly urged then-Speaker Perez to challenge Uthmeier in the GOP primary, hoping to supplant a DeSantis ally; Perez demurred, and Uthmeier won the nomination unopposed.) To make his mark, Uthmeier has filed several high-profile and politically charged lawsuits — for instance, he sued Starbucks over its corporate diversity politics (the company recently settled ), and Pfizer about the safety of its Covid-19 vaccine
He’s also subpoenaed the NFL over its “Rooney Rule,” which requires teams to interview minority candidates for top coaching and operations jobs
He’s also become the face of the administration’s challenge to the AI industry
In April, Uthmeier stood in front of a podium with an “Investigating OpenAI” sign, announcing he’d opened a criminal investigation into the company

The impetus was a shooting at Florida State University last year that killed two people and injured six others; the accused shooter had consulted ChatGPT about various topics related to his plans hours before the attack. “If ChatGPT were a person, it would be facing charges for murder,” Uthmeier said then. “This criminal investigation will determine whether OpenAI bears criminal responsibility for ChatGPT’s actions.” There have been no criminal charges yet

But in June, Uthmeier filed a wide-ranging civil lawsuit against OpenAI , alleging deceptive business practices, negligence, fraudulent misrepresentation, and other legal violations, because the company marketed ChatGPT as safe when they knew it could be quite dangerous

title: A door to single-payer healthcare could open after November 3
excerpt: Protest signs seen at protect Medicaid lights up Capitol amid budget showdown, on May 7, 2025, in Washington, DC. | Leigh Vogel/Getty Images for Caring Across G
body: Protest signs seen at protect Medicaid lights up Capitol amid budget showdown, on May 7, 2025, in Washington, DC. | Leigh Vogel/Getty Images for Caring Across Generations Twelve years ago, Vermont Democrats tried to make their state the first in the nation to have a single-payer government-financed healthcare system — a bold experiment to push the limits of American health coverage when Obamacare was just being launched
Their plan failed , and rebooting it became politically impossible, even in Vermont: The Democrats lost the governorship to Republican Phil Scott for what turned out to be a decade
A progressive political newcomer named Amanda Janoo is taking on Scott in what polls show is a tight governor’s race

And if she wins, the state could be poised to try a whole new national experiment: One of Janoo’s central campaign promises is to create a pioneering health system where the state pays the full tab for primary and preventive care, while leaving the rest to the existing system

Key takeaways Amanda Janoo, the Democratic nominee for governor of Vermont, wants to move primary and preventive healthcare to a single-payer system — where the state would pay providers for such care, make it free for patients, and cut insurers out
Previous attempts to pass or enact full single-payer systems have failed at the state level, including in Vermont in 2014
Janoo is trying to focus first on this one relatively smaller slice of the health system, but hopes it could be a starting point to full single-payer reform eventually
Yet even this more limited reform faces difficult political and practical challenges
Janoo’s candidacy is an example of the policy experiments that are becoming possible nationwide in a projected “blue wave” year, when Democrats could sweep into power in a number of states
But in the healthcare universe, her plan is also an example of how even progressive policy idealists are trying to learn from past failures and focus on what they think can actually be achieved
Compared to the sweeping ambition of Vermont’s 2014 effort, or Bernie Sanders’s signature “Medicare-for-all” idea, Janoo’s proposal for single-payer has very specific limits

Under Janoo’s proposal for “universal primary and preventive care” (she typically avoids the term “single-payer”), the state government would pay for Vermonters seeing primary care providers such as doctors and nurse practitioners
This government coverage would be universal and free for patients, and insurance companies would be cut out
However, other parts of the health system — such as hospitals, specialists, and prescription drug companies — would remain under the existing insurance system, for now
Every effort so far to enact full single-payer at the state level has failed — even in blue states , bills and ballot initiatives have regularly gone down to defeat
Vermont’s previous single-payer experiment made it the furthest — it was signed into law but abandoned before being implemented, when the governor concluded it was unworkable
Wherever it’s gained steam, politicians and voters have blanched at the high costs of moving their health systems onto state budgets, and the high taxes that would be necessary to fund them

Now, Janoo is making an attempt to refurbish single-payer as something more achievable, by cutting off a smaller slice of it. “I think it’s clear at this point that a profit-oriented healthcare system is a terrible idea,” Janoo told me in an interview on Monday
But after assessing that the state budget made it “unrealistic” to do single-payer immediately, she concluded, “we could do universal primary and preventive care,” financed by a tax on the wealthiest
Indeed, single-payer for primary care seems more achievable precisely because primary care is a relatively less expensive part of the healthcare system

But Janoo hopes it will pay major dividends — that better preventive care will improve Vermonters’ health, reducing costs elsewhere in the system by, for instance, making some hospital visits unnecessary
In speaking to health policy experts about this idea, I heard much sympathy for the goal of universal primary care, but many questions about the details

Would Janoo’s plan be sufficient to bring more primary care doctors to Vermont — and, not unrelatedly, would it pay them more? Would her hoped-for cost savings from preventive care actually materialize? Is picking up the tab for a relatively less expensive part of the healthcare system the best use of sparse state funding? These questions are becoming national ones, as healthcare gains traction as a political issue again

It isn’t just Vermont where primary care reform ideas are gaining steam: Democrats in Minnesota , Washington state, and elsewhere have discussed them. “There is growing interest in a number of states across the country in doing a universal primary care for all program,” Kevin Grumbach, a family physician and a professor of family and community medicine at the University of California San Francisco, told me
Even Scott, Janoo’s opponent, signed a law calling for a study of universal primary care
One dividing line emerging, though, is whether to keep insurers involved, or to clear them out with a single-payer system, as Janoo wants
Insurers are unpopular with the public, but they can be a formidable political opponent when they argue that the benefits voters currently enjoy might be lost
Scott has said that the idea of universal primary care is appealing — but that if universal is “just code for single payer, I’m not interested

We’ve already been through that.” Yet Janoo is hoping that single-payer for primary care will be a stepping stone — a trial run for eventually making the rest of the state’s health system single-payer down the road. “I think about this often,” Janoo told me. “How do you build the new system as you transition the old — or hospice the old?” Amanda Janoo is tired of “corporate neoliberal bullshit” Janoo has long been an unorthodox economic policy thinker

Her rise is part of a broader trend in which progressives and leftists are winning primaries and gaining influence in the Democratic Party — but she doesn’t fit the prototype of the democratic socialist candidates in New York City , Colorado , and elsewhere who’ve gotten much attention this year
Instead, she comes from a different strand of the left, a movement based on a dissident strain of economics and openly skeptical of the benefits of economic growth

Dating back to when she graduated from college in 2010, in the aftermath of the financial crisis, she was part of a younger cohort rebelling against what seemed the glaring failures of the economic establishment. “The one thing coming out of university I was clear on was that neoliberalism was the worst,” Janoo said on a podcast last year. “This whole idea that governments should just take a hands-off approach to the economy and trust in sort of the disciplinary powers of the global free market to lead them to infinite growth seemed highly problematic and very anti-democratic.” So for graduate school, Janoo attended Cambridge to study development economics under the “heterodox” economist Ha-Joon Chang
She then spent several years working abroad in international development for the United Nations and other organizations, before moving back to Vermont and working as an economic policy consultant

In recent years, Janoo became deeply involved with the “ well-being economy ” movement: an international group of advocates, academics, and experts who criticize what they deem modern capitalism’s obsession with economic growth, and say the “well-being” of humans and the environment should be prioritized instead

They overlap with the “ degrowth ” movement, which outright argues economic growth should be reduced; last year, Janoo led a workshop at a DeGrowth Institute event on “Degrowth Policy Design.” Trump’s return to power horrified Janoo. “I’m feeling angry about the rise of fascism and the growing threat of world war, because I feel like we don’t have time for this shit,” she said in a speech at an environmental event last year. ”The planet is on fire and ecosystems are collapsing, and that should really be the focus of all of our attention.” But, she said, “I believe I was born in this moment of history for a reason” and vowed “to fight for democracy — for life.” So Janoo decided to jump in the race for governor of Vermont

While she is not running on a degrowth platform, her campaign is deeply informed by aspects of the movement’s thought: skepticism about growth’s benefits, a sense that untrammeled capitalism is leading the world to disaster, and that localism provides a better way

For instance, candidates for governor typically pledge that they’d help bring business investment in, but Janoo said in a July debate : “A lot of the problems we’re facing is because we focus so much on attracting external business.”  “Our economy is not super-diversified, and it is not really centered in the most essential kinds of goods and services you want to make sure people have access to no matter what happens — because honestly, things are bad now and they’re going to get worse,” Janoo told me. “I feel a little bit like a collective prepper right now
My motto is, protect what we love, produce what we need.” In the Democratic primary, Janoo’s opponent, Aly Richards, had closer ties to the party establishment and led in fundraising

But Janoo ran as a progressive outsider; she promised to advance a “more economically populist vision” instead of “corporate neoliberal bullshit.” Her health plan became a point of contrast with Richards, who said she wouldn’t run on “ magical thinking ,” and that she wanted a version of universal primary care that would keep insurance companies involved
Janoo won the primary by 2.5 percentage points

body: Style of emceeing based on high-octane, ad-libbed vocals has flourished thanks to its unique way of captivating crowds For the 2015 freshmen cohort of the history degree programme at the University of Lagos, their classmate’s first-semester presentation was so captivating that they began calling him Toby Shang, after the 16th-century Chinese dynasty he had focused on
His crowd engagement that day had been harnessed from his high school days as a ginger-man (energiser) in a three-man band and as a private tutor
By his final year at university, his viral catchphrases and infectious energy had resulted in a hit song, Shedibalabala
Today, he is one of the self-acclaimed “evangelists and pioneers” in the Afrobeats sub-genre some are now calling Afrohype or lamba
